A user can change the properties of some or all of the
tasks in a running job by pushing a new job conﬁguration
to Borg, and then instructing Borg to update the tasks to
the new speciﬁcation. This acts as a lightweight, non-atomic
transaction that can easily be undone until it is closed (com-
mitted). Updates are generally done in a rolling fashion, and
a limit can be imposed on the number of task disruptions
2 Borg manages the available ports on a machine and allocates them to tasks.


=== PDF page 3 ===
(reschedules or preemptions) an update causes; any changes
that would cause more disruptions are skipped.
Some task updates (e.g., pushing a new binary) will al-
ways require the task to be restarted; some (e.g., increasing
resource requirements or changing constraints) might make
the task no longer ﬁt on the machine, and cause it to be
stopped and rescheduled; and some (e.g., changing priority)
can always be done without restarting or moving the task.
Tasks can ask to be notiﬁed via a Unix SIGTERM sig-
nal before they are preempted by a SIGKILL, so they have
time to clean up, save state, ﬁnish any currently-executing
requests, and decline new ones. The actual notice may be
less if the preemptor sets a delay bound. In practice, a notice
is delivered about 80% of the time.
2.4
Allocs
A Borg alloc (short for allocation) is a reserved set of re-
sources on a machine in which one or more tasks can be
run; the resources remain assigned whether or not they are
used. Allocs can be used to set resources aside for future
tasks, to retain resources between stopping a task and start-
ing it again, and to gather tasks from different jobs onto the
same machine – e.g., a web server instance and an associ-
ated logsaver task that copies the server’s URL logs from
the local disk to a distributed ﬁle system. The resources of
an alloc are treated in a similar way to the resources of a ma-
chine; multiple tasks running inside one share its resources.
If an alloc must be relocated to another machine, its tasks are
rescheduled with it.
An alloc set is like a job: it is a group of allocs that reserve
resources on multiple machines. Once an alloc set has been
created, one or more jobs can be submitted to run in it. For
brevity, we will generally use “task” to refer to an alloc or a
top-level task (one outside an alloc) and “job” to refer to a
job or alloc set.
2.5
Priority, quota, and admission control
What happens when more work shows up than can be ac-
commodated? Our solutions for this are priority and quota.
Every job has a priority, a small positive integer. A high-
priority task can obtain resources at the expense of a lower-
priority one, even if that involves preempting (killing) the
latter. Borg deﬁnes non-overlapping priority bands for dif-
ferent uses, including (in decreasing-priority order): moni-
toring, production, batch, and best eﬀort (also known as
testing or free). For this paper, prod jobs are the ones in the
monitoring and production bands.
Although a preempted task will often be rescheduled
elsewhere in the cell, preemption cascades could occur if
a high-priority task bumped out a slightly lower-priority
one, which bumped out another slightly-lower priority task,
and so on. To eliminate most of this, we disallow tasks in
the production priority band to preempt one another. Fine-
grained priorities are still useful in other circumstances –
e.g., MapReduce master tasks run at a slightly higher priority
than the workers they control, to improve their reliability.
Priority expresses relative importance for jobs that are
running or waiting to run in a cell. Quota is used to decide
which jobs to admit for scheduling. Quota is expressed as
a vector of resource quantities (CPU, RAM, disk, etc.) at a
given priority, for a period of time (typically months). The
quantities specify the maximum amount of resources that
a user’s job requests can ask for at a time (e.g., “20 TiB
of RAM at prod priority from now until the end of July
in cell xx”). Quota-checking is part of admission control,
not scheduling: jobs with insufﬁcient quota are immediately
rejected upon submission.
Higher-priority quota costs more than quota at lower-
priority. Production-priority quota is limited to the actual
resources available in the cell, so that a user who submits
a production-priority job that ﬁts in their quota can expect it
to run, modulo fragmentation and constraints. Even though
we encourage users to purchase no more quota than they
need, many users overbuy because it insulates them against
future shortages when their application’s user base grows.
We respond to this by over-selling quota at lower-priority
levels: every user has inﬁnite quota at priority zero, although
this is frequently hard to exercise because resources are over-
subscribed. A low-priority job may be admitted but remain
pending (unscheduled) due to insufﬁcient resources.
Quota allocation is handled outside of Borg, and is inti-
mately tied to our physical capacity planning, whose results
are reﬂected in the price and availability of quota in differ-
ent datacenters. User jobs are admitted only if they have suf-
ﬁcient quota at the required priority. The use of quota re-
duces the need for policies like Dominant Resource Fairness
(DRF) [29, 35, 36, 66].
Borg has a capability system that gives special privileges
to some users; for example, allowing administrators to delete
or modify any job in the cell, or allowing a user to access
restricted kernel features or Borg behaviors such as disabling
resource estimation (§5.5) on their jobs.
2.6
Naming and monitoring
It’s not enough to create and place tasks: a service’s clients
and other systems need to be able to ﬁnd them, even after
they are relocated to a new machine. To enable this, Borg
creates a stable “Borg name service” (BNS) name for each
task that includes the cell name, job name, and task number.
Borg writes the task’s hostname and port into a consistent,
highly-available ﬁle in Chubby [14] with this name, which
is used by our RPC system to ﬁnd the task endpoint. The
BNS name also forms the basis of the task’s DNS name,
so the ﬁftieth task in job jfoo owned by user ubar in cell
cc would be reachable via 50.jfoo.ubar.cc.borg.google.com.
Borg also writes job size and task health information into
Chubby whenever it changes, so load balancers can see
where to route requests to.


=== PDF page 4 ===
Almost every task run under Borg contains a built-in
HTTP server that publishes information about the health of
the task and thousands of performance metrics (e.g., RPC
latencies). Borg monitors the health-check URL and restarts
tasks that do not respond promptly or return an HTTP er-
ror code. Other data is tracked by monitoring tools for dash-
boards and alerts on service level objective (SLO) violations.
A service called Sigma provides a web-based user inter-
face (UI) through which a user can examine the state of all
their jobs, a particular cell, or drill down to individual jobs
and tasks to examine their resource behavior, detailed logs,
execution history, and eventual fate. Our applications gener-
ate voluminous logs; these are automatically rotated to avoid
running out of disk space, and preserved for a while after the
task’s exit to assist with debugging. If a job is not running
Borg provides a “why pending?” annotation, together with
guidance on how to modify the job’s resource requests to
better ﬁt the cell. We publish guidelines for “conforming”
resource shapes that are likely to schedule easily.
Borg records all job submissions and task events, as well
as detailed per-task resource usage information in Infrastore,
a scalable read-only data store with an interactive SQL-like
interface via Dremel [61]. This data is used for usage-based
charging, debugging job and system failures, and long-term
capacity planning. It also provided the data for the Google
cluster workload trace [80].
All of these features help users to understand and debug
the behavior of Borg and their jobs, and help our SREs
manage a few tens of thousands of machines per person.
3.
Borg architecture
A Borg cell consists of a set of machines, a logically central-
ized controller called the Borgmaster, and an agent process
called the Borglet that runs on each machine in a cell (see
Figure 1). All components of Borg are written in C++.
3.1
Borgmaster
Each cell’s Borgmaster consists of two processes: the main
Borgmaster process and a separate scheduler (§3.2). The
main Borgmaster process handles client RPCs that either
mutate state (e.g., create job) or provide read-only access
to data (e.g., lookup job). It also manages state machines
for all of the objects in the system (machines, tasks, allocs,
etc.), communicates with the Borglets, and offers a web UI
as a backup to Sigma.
The Borgmaster is logically a single process but is ac-
tually replicated ﬁve times. Each replica maintains an in-
memory copy of most of the state of the cell, and this state is
also recorded in a highly-available, distributed, Paxos-based
store [55] on the replicas’ local disks. A single elected mas-
ter per cell serves both as the Paxos leader and the state
mutator, handling all operations that change the cell’s state,
such as submitting a job or terminating a task on a ma-
chine. A master is elected (using Paxos) when the cell is
brought up and whenever the elected master fails; it acquires
a Chubby lock so other systems can ﬁnd it. Electing a master
and failing-over to the new one typically takes about 10 s, but
can take up to a minute in a big cell because some in-memory
state has to be reconstructed. When a replica recovers from
an outage, it dynamically re-synchronizes its state from other
Paxos replicas that are up-to-date.
The Borgmaster’s state at a point in time is called a
checkpoint, and takes the form of a periodic snapshot plus a
change log kept in the Paxos store. Checkpoints have many
uses, including restoring a Borgmaster’s state to an arbitrary
point in the past (e.g., just before accepting a request that
triggered a software defect in Borg so it can be debugged);
ﬁxing it by hand in extremis; building a persistent log of
events for future queries; and ofﬂine simulations.
A high-ﬁdelity Borgmaster simulator called Fauxmaster
can be used to read checkpoint ﬁles, and contains a complete
copy of the production Borgmaster code, with stubbed-out
interfaces to the Borglets. It accepts RPCs to make state ma-
chine changes and perform operations, such as “schedule all
pending tasks”, and we use it to debug failures, by interact-
ing with it as if it were a live Borgmaster, with simulated
Borglets replaying real interactions from the checkpoint ﬁle.
A user can step through and observe the changes to the sys-
tem state that actually occurred in the past. Fauxmaster is
also useful for capacity planning (“how many new jobs of
this type would ﬁt?”), as well as sanity checks before mak-
ing a change to a cell’s conﬁguration (“will this change evict
any important jobs?”).
3.2
Scheduling
When a job is submitted, the Borgmaster records it persis-
tently in the Paxos store and adds the job’s tasks to the pend-
ing queue. This is scanned asynchronously by the scheduler,
which assigns tasks to machines if there are sufﬁcient avail-
able resources that meet the job’s constraints. (The sched-
uler primarily operates on tasks, not jobs.) The scan pro-
ceeds from high to low priority, modulated by a round-robin
scheme within a priority to ensure fairness across users and
avoid head-of-line blocking behind a large job. The schedul-
ing algorithm has two parts: feasibility checking, to ﬁnd ma-
chines on which the task could run, and scoring, which picks
one of the feasible machines.
In feasibility checking, the scheduler ﬁnds a set of ma-
chines that meet the task’s constraints and also have enough
“available” resources – which includes resources assigned
to lower-priority tasks that can be evicted. In scoring, the
scheduler determines the “goodness” of each feasible ma-
chine. The score takes into account user-speciﬁed prefer-
ences, but is mostly driven by built-in criteria such as mini-
mizing the number and priority of preempted tasks, picking
machines that already have a copy of the task’s packages,
spreading tasks across power and failure domains, and pack-
ing quality including putting a mix of high and low priority


=== PDF page 5 ===
tasks onto a single machine to allow the high-priority ones
to expand in a load spike.
Borg originally used a variant of E-PVM [4] for scoring,
which generates a single cost value across heterogeneous
resources and minimizes the change in cost when placing
a task. In practice, E-PVM ends up spreading load across
all the machines, leaving headroom for load spikes – but at
the expense of increased fragmentation, especially for large
tasks that need most of the machine; we sometimes call this
“worst ﬁt”.
The opposite end of the spectrum is “best ﬁt”, which tries
to ﬁll machines as tightly as possible. This leaves some ma-
chines empty of user jobs (they still run storage servers), so
placing large tasks is straightforward, but the tight packing
penalizes any mis-estimations in resource requirements by
users or Borg. This hurts applications with bursty loads, and
is particularly bad for batch jobs which specify low CPU
needs so they can schedule easily and try to run opportunis-
tically in unused resources: 20% of non-prod tasks request
less than 0.1 CPU cores.
Our current scoring model is a hybrid one that tries to
reduce the amount of stranded resources – ones that cannot
be used because another resource on the machine is fully
allocated. It provides about 3–5% better packing efﬁciency
(deﬁned in [78]) than best ﬁt for our workloads.
If the machine selected by the scoring phase doesn’t have
enough available resources to ﬁt the new task, Borg preempts
(kills) lower-priority tasks, from lowest to highest priority,
until it does. We add the preempted tasks to the scheduler’s
pending queue, rather than migrate or hibernate them.3
Task startup latency (the time from job submission to
a task running) is an area that has received and continues
to receive signiﬁcant attention. It is highly variable, with
the median typically about 25 s. Package installation takes
about 80% of the total: one of the known bottlenecks is
contention for the local disk where packages are written to.
To reduce task startup time, the scheduler prefers to assign
tasks to machines that already have the necessary packages
(programs and data) installed: most packages are immutable
and so can be shared and cached. (This is the only form of
data locality supported by the Borg scheduler.) In addition,
Borg distributes packages to machines in parallel using tree-
and torrent-like protocols.
Additionally, the scheduler uses several techniques to let
it scale up to cells with tens of thousands of machines (§3.4).
3.3
Borglet
The Borglet is a local Borg agent that is present on every
machine in a cell. It starts and stops tasks; restarts them if
they fail; manages local resources by manipulating OS ker-
nel settings; rolls over debug logs; and reports the state of the
machine to the Borgmaster and other monitoring systems.
3 Exception: tasks that provide virtual machines for Google Compute En-
gine users are migrated.
The Borgmaster polls each Borglet every few seconds to
retrieve the machine’s current state and send it any outstand-
ing requests. This gives Borgmaster control over the rate of
communication, avoids the need for an explicit ﬂow control
mechanism, and prevents recovery storms [9].
The elected master is responsible for preparing messages
to send to the Borglets and for updating the cell’s state with
their responses. For performance scalability, each Borgmas-
ter replica runs a stateless link shard to handle the communi-
cation with some of the Borglets; the partitioning is recalcu-
lated whenever a Borgmaster election occurs. For resiliency,
the Borglet always reports its full state, but the link shards
aggregate and compress this information by reporting only
differences to the state machines, to reduce the update load
at the elected master.
If a Borglet does not respond to several poll messages its
machine is marked as down and any tasks it was running
are rescheduled on other machines. If communication is
restored the Borgmaster tells the Borglet to kill those tasks
that have been rescheduled, to avoid duplicates. A Borglet
continues normal operation even if it loses contact with the
Borgmaster, so currently-running tasks and services stay up
even if all Borgmaster replicas fail.
3.4
Scalability
We are not sure where the ultimate scalability limit to Borg’s
centralized architecture will come from; so far, every time
we have approached a limit, we’ve managed to eliminate it.
A single Borgmaster can manage many thousands of ma-
chines in a cell, and several cells have arrival rates above
10 000 tasks per minute. A busy Borgmaster uses 10–14
CPU cores and up to 50 GiB RAM. We use several tech-
niques to achieve this scale.
Early versions of Borgmaster had a simple, synchronous
loop that accepted requests, scheduled tasks, and commu-
nicated with Borglets. To handle larger cells, we split the
scheduler into a separate process so it could operate in paral-
lel with the other Borgmaster functions that are replicated for
failure tolerance. A scheduler replica operates on a cached
copy of the cell state. It repeatedly: retrieves state changes
from the elected master (including both assigned and pend-
ing work); updates its local copy; does a scheduling pass
to assign tasks; and informs the elected master of those as-
signments. The master will accept and apply these assign-
ments unless they are inappropriate (e.g., based on out of
date state), which will cause them to be reconsidered in the
scheduler’s next pass. This is quite similar in spirit to the
optimistic concurrency control used in Omega [69], and in-
deed we recently added the ability for Borg to use different
schedulers for different workload types.
To improve response times, we added separate threads
to talk to the Borglets and respond to read-only RPCs. For
greater performance, we sharded (partitioned) these func-
tions across the ﬁve Borgmaster replicas §3.3. Together,

Several things make the Borg scheduler more scalable:
Score caching: Evaluating feasibility and scoring a ma-
chine is expensive, so Borg caches the scores until the prop-
erties of the machine or task change – e.g., a task on the ma-
chine terminates, an attribute is altered, or a task’s require-
ments change. Ignoring small changes in resource quantities
reduces cache invalidations.
Equivalence classes: Tasks in a Borg job usually have
identical requirements and constraints, so rather than deter-
mining feasibility for every pending task on every machine,
and scoring all the feasible machines, Borg only does fea-
sibility and scoring for one task per equivalence class – a
group of tasks with identical requirements.
Relaxed randomization: It is wasteful to calculate fea-
sibility and scores for all the machines in a large cell, so the
scheduler examines machines in a random order until it has
found “enough” feasible machines to score, and then selects
the best within that set. This reduces the amount of scoring
and cache invalidations needed when tasks enter and leave
the system, and speeds up assignment of tasks to machines.
Relaxed randomization is somewhat akin to the batch sam-
pling of Sparrow [65] while also handling priorities, preemp-
tions, heterogeneity and the costs of package installation.
In our experiments (§5), scheduling a cell’s entire work-
load from scratch typically took a few hundred seconds, but
did not ﬁnish after more than 3 days when the above tech-
niques were disabled. Normally, though, an online schedul-
ing pass over the pending queue completes in less than half
a second.
4.
Availability
Failures are the norm in large scale systems [10, 11, 22].
Figure 3 provides a breakdown of task eviction causes in
15 sample cells. Applications that run on Borg are expected
to handle such events, using techniques such as replication,
storing persistent state in a distributed ﬁle system, and (if
appropriate) taking occasional checkpoints. Even so, we try
to mitigate the impact of these events. For example, Borg:
• automatically reschedules evicted tasks, on a new ma-
chine if necessary;
• reduces correlated failures by spreading tasks of a job
across failure domains such as machines, racks, and
power domains;
• limits the allowed rate of task disruptions and the number
of tasks from a job that can be simultaneously down

A key design feature in Borg is that already-running tasks
continue to run even if the Borgmaster or a task’s Borglet
goes down. But keeping the master up is still important
because when it is down new jobs cannot be submitted
or existing ones updated, and tasks from failed machines
cannot be rescheduled.
Borgmaster uses a combination of techniques that enable
it to achieve 99.99% availability in practice: replication for
machine failures; admission control to avoid overload; and
deploying instances using simple, low-level tools to mini-
mize external dependencies. Each cell is independent of the
others to minimize the chance of correlated operator errors
and failure propagation. These goals, not scalability limita-
tions, are the primary argument against larger cells.
5.
Utilization
One of Borg’s primary goals is to make efﬁcient use of
Google’s ﬂeet of machines, which represents a signiﬁcant
ﬁnancial investment: increasing utilization by a few percent-
age points can save millions of dollars. This section dis-
cusses and evaluates some of the policies and techniques that
Borg uses to do so.

5.1
Evaluation methodology
Our jobs have placement constraints and need to handle rare
workload spikes, our machines are heterogenous, and we
run batch jobs in resources reclaimed from service jobs. So,
to evaluate our policy choices we needed a more sophisti-
cated metric than “average utilization”. After much exper-
imentation we picked cell compaction: given a workload,
we found out how small a cell it could be ﬁtted into by
removing machines until the workload no longer ﬁtted, re-
peatedly re-packing the workload from scratch to ensure that
we didn’t get hung up on an unlucky conﬁguration. This
provided clean termination conditions and facilitated auto-
mated comparisons without the pitfalls of synthetic work-
load generation and modeling [31]. A quantitative compari-
son of evaluation techniques can be found in [78]: the details
are surprisingly subtle.
It wasn’t possible to perform experiments on live produc-
tion cells, but we used Fauxmaster to obtain high-ﬁdelity
simulation results, using data from real production cells
and workloads, including all their constraints, actual lim-
its, reservations, and usage data (§5.5). This data came
from Borg checkpoints taken on Wednesday 2014-10-01
14:00 PDT. (Other checkpoints produced similar results.)
We picked 15 Borg cells to report on by ﬁrst eliminating
special-purpose, test, and small (< 5000 machines) cells,
and then sampled the remaining population to achieve a
roughly even spread across the range of sizes.
To maintain machine heterogeneity in the compacted cell
we randomly selected machines to remove. To maintain
workload heterogeneity, we kept it all, except for server and
storage tasks tied to a particular machine (e.g., the Borglets).
We changed hard constraints to soft ones for jobs larger than
half the original cell size, and allowed up to 0.2% tasks to go
pending if they were very “picky” and could only be placed
on a handful of machines; extensive experiments showed
that this produced repeatable results with low variance. If

5.2
Cell sharing
Nearly all of our machines run both prod and non-prod tasks
at the same time: 98% of the machines in shared Borg cells,
83% across the entire set of machines managed by Borg. (We
have a few dedicated cells for special uses.)
Since many other organizations run user-facing and batch
jobs in separate clusters, we examined what would happen if
we did the same. Figure 5 shows that segregating prod and
non-prod work would need 20–30% more machines in the
median cell to run our workload. That’s because prod jobs
usually reserve resources to handle rare workload spikes, but
don’t use these resources most of the time. Borg reclaims the
unused resources (§5.5) to run much of the non-prod work,
so we need fewer machines overall.
Most Borg cells are shared by thousands of users. Figure
6 shows why. For this test, we split off a user’s workload
into a new cell if they consumed at least 10 TiB of mem-
ory (or 100 TiB). Our existing policy looks good: even with
the larger threshold, we would need 2–16× as many cells,
and 20–150% additional machines. Once again, pooling re-
sources signiﬁcantly reduces costs.
But perhaps packing unrelated users and job types onto
the same machines results in CPU interference, and so we
would need more machines to compensate? To assess this,
we looked at how the CPI (cycles per instruction) changed
for tasks in different environments running on the same ma-
chine type with the same clock speed. Under these condi-
tions, CPI values are comparable and can be used as a proxy
for performance interference, since a doubling of CPI dou-
bles the runtime of a CPU-bound program. The data was
gathered from ∼12000 randomly selected prod tasks over
a week, counting cycles and instructions over a 5 minute in-
terval using the hardware proﬁling infrastructure described
in [83], and weighting samples so that every second of CPU
time is counted equally. The results were not clear-cut.
(1) We found that CPI was positively correlated with
two measurements over the same time interval: the overall
CPU usage on the machine, and (largely independently) the
number of tasks on the machine; adding a task to a machine
increases the CPI of other tasks by 0.3% (using a linear
model ﬁtted to the data); increasing machine CPU usage by
10% increases CPI by less than 2%. But even though the
correlations are statistically signiﬁcant, they only explain 5%
of the variance we saw in CPI measurements; other factors
dominate, such as inherent differences in applications and
speciﬁc interference patterns [24, 83].
(2) Comparing the CPIs we sampled from shared cells to
ones from a few dedicated cells with less diverse applica-
tions, we saw a mean CPI of 1.58 (σ = 0.35) in shared cells
and a mean of 1.53 (σ = 0.32) in dedicated cells – i.e., CPU
performance is about 3% worse in shared cells.
(3) To address the concern that applications in different
cells might have different workloads, or even suffer selection
bias (maybe programs that are more sensitive to interference
had been moved to dedicated cells), we looked at the CPI of
the Borglet, which runs on all the machines in both types of
cell. We found it had a CPI of 1.20 (σ = 0.29) in dedicated
cells and 1.43 (σ = 0.45) in shared ones, suggesting that
it runs 1.19× as fast in a dedicated cell as in a shared
one, although this over-weights the effect of lightly loaded
machines, slightly biasing the result in favor of dedicated
cells.

5.5
Resource reclamation
A job can specify a resource limit – an upper bound on the
resources that each task should be granted. The limit is used
by Borg to determine if the user has enough quota to admit
the job, and to determine if a particular machine has enough
free resources to schedule the task. Just as there are users
who buy more quota than they need, there are users who
request more resources than their tasks will use, because
Borg will normally kill a task that tries to use more RAM
or disk space than it requested, or throttle CPU to what it
asked for. In addition, some tasks occasionally need to use
all their resources (e.g., at peak times of day or while coping
with a denial-of-service attack), but most of the time do not.
Rather than waste allocated resources that are not cur-
rently being consumed, we estimate how many resources a
task will use and reclaim the rest for work that can tolerate
lower-quality resources, such as batch jobs. This whole pro-
cess is called resource reclamation. The estimate is called
the task’s reservation, and is computed by the Borgmas-
ter every few seconds, using ﬁne-grained usage (resource-
consumption) information captured by the Borglet. The ini-
tial reservation is set equal to the resource request (the limit);
after 300 s, to allow for startup transients, it decays slowly
towards the actual usage plus a safety margin. The reserva-
tion is rapidly increased if the usage exceeds it.
The Borg scheduler uses limits to calculate feasibility
(§3.2) for prod tasks,4 so they never rely on reclaimed re-
sources and aren’t exposed to resource oversubscription; for
non-prod tasks, it uses the reservations of existing tasks so
the new tasks can be scheduled into reclaimed resources.
A machine may run out of resources at runtime if the
reservations (predictions) are wrong – even if all tasks use

Figure 10 shows that many more machines would be
required without resource reclamation. About 20% of the
workload (§6.2) runs in reclaimed resources in a median cell.
We can see more details in Figure 11, which shows the
ratio of reservations and usage to limits. A task that exceeds
its memory limit will be the ﬁrst to be preempted if resources
are needed, regardless of its priority, so it is rare for tasks
to exceed their memory limit. On the other hand, CPU can
readily be throttled, so short-term spikes can push usage
above reservation fairly harmlessly.
Figure 11 suggests that resource reclamation may be un-
necessarily conservative: there is signiﬁcant area between
the reservation and usage lines. To test this, we picked a live
production cell and adjusted the parameters of its resource
estimation algorithm to an aggressive setting for a week by
reducing the safety margin, and then to an medium setting
that was mid-way between the baseline and aggressive set-
tings for the next week, and then reverted to the baseline.

6.
Isolation
50% of our machines run 9 or more tasks; a 90%ile machine
has about 25 tasks and will be running about 4500 threads
[83]. Although sharing machines between applications in-
creases utilization, it also requires good mechanisms to pre-
vent tasks from interfering with one another. This applies to
both security and performance.
6.1
Security isolation
We use a Linux chroot jail as the primary security isolation
mechanism between multiple tasks on the same machine. To
allow remote debugging, we used to distribute (and rescind)
ssh keys automatically to give a user access to a machine
only while it was running tasks for the user. For most users,
this has been replaced by the borgssh command, which col-
laborates with the Borglet to construct an ssh connection to
a shell that runs in the same chroot and cgroup as the task,
locking down access even more tightly.
VMs and security sandboxing techniques are used to run
external software by Google’s AppEngine (GAE) [38] and
Google Compute Engine (GCE). We run each hosted VM in
a KVM process [54] that runs as a Borg task.
6.2
Performance isolation
Early versions of Borglet had relatively primitive resource
isolation enforcement: post-hoc usage checking of memory,
disk space and CPU cycles, combined with termination of
tasks that used too much memory or disk and aggressive ap-
plication of Linux’s CPU priorities to rein in tasks that used
too much CPU. But it was still too easy for rogue tasks to af-
fect the performance of other tasks on the machine, so some
users inﬂated their resource requests to reduce the number of
tasks that Borg could co-schedule with theirs, thus decreas-
ing utilization. Resource reclamation could claw back some
of the surplus, but not all, because of the safety margins in-
volved. In the most extreme cases, users petitioned to use
dedicated machines or cells.
Now, all Borg tasks run inside a Linux cgroup-based re-
source container [17, 58, 62] and the Borglet manipulates the
container settings, giving much improved control because
the OS kernel is in the loop. Even so, occasional low-level
resource interference (e.g., memory bandwidth or L3 cache
pollution) still happens, as in [60, 83].
5 The anomaly at the end of week 3 is unrelated to this experiment.
To help with overload and overcommitment, Borg tasks
have an application class or appclass. The most important
distinction is between the latency-sensitive (LS) appclasses
and the rest, which we call batch in this paper. LS tasks are
used for user-facing applications and shared infrastructure
services that require fast response to requests. High-priority
LS tasks receive the best treatment, and are capable of tem-
porarily starving batch tasks for several seconds at a time.
A second split is between compressible resources (e.g.,
CPU cycles, disk I/O bandwidth) that are rate-based and
can be reclaimed from a task by decreasing its quality of
service without killing it; and non-compressible resources
(e.g., memory, disk space) which generally cannot be re-
claimed without killing the task. If a machine runs out of
non-compressible resources, the Borglet immediately termi-
nates tasks, from lowest to highest priority, until the remain-
ing reservations can be met. If the machine runs out of com-
pressible resources, the Borglet throttles usage (favoring LS
tasks) so that short load spikes can be handled without killing
any tasks. If things do not improve, Borgmaster will remove
one or more tasks from the machine.
A user-space control loop in the Borglet assigns mem-
ory to containers based on predicted future usage (for prod
tasks) or on memory pressure (for non-prod ones); handles
Out-of-Memory (OOM) events from the kernel; and kills
tasks when they try to allocate beyond their memory lim-
its, or when an over-committed machine actually runs out
of memory. Linux’s eager ﬁle-caching signiﬁcantly compli-
cates the implementation because of the need for accurate
memory-accounting.
To improve performance isolation, LS tasks can reserve
entire physical CPU cores, which stops other LS tasks from
using them. Batch tasks are permitted to run on any core,
but they are given tiny scheduler shares relative to the LS
tasks. The Borglet dynamically adjusts the resource caps of
greedy LS tasks in order to ensure that they do not starve
batch tasks for multiple minutes, selectively applying CFS
bandwidth control when needed [75]; shares are insufﬁcient
because we have multiple priority levels.
Like Leverich [56], we found that the standard Linux
CPU scheduler (CFS) required substantial tuning to support
both low latency and high utilization. To reduce schedul-
ing delays, our version of CFS uses extended per-cgroup
load history [16], allows preemption of batch tasks by LS
tasks, and reduces the scheduling quantum when multiple LS
tasks are runnable on a CPU. Fortunately, many of our ap-
plications use a thread-per-request model, which mitigates
the effects of persistent load imbalances. We sparingly use
cpusets to allocate CPU cores to applications with particu-
larly tight latency requirements. Some results of these efforts
are shown in Figure 13. Work continues in this area, adding
thread placement and CPU management that is NUMA-,
hyperthreading-, and power-aware (e.g., [81]), and improv-
ing the control ﬁdelity of the Borglet.


=== PDF page 12 ===
Tasks are permitted to consume resources up to their
limit. Most of them are allowed to go beyond that for com-
pressible resources like CPU, to take advantage of unused
(slack) resources. Only 5% of LS tasks disable this, presum-
ably to get better predictability; fewer than 1% of batch tasks
do. Using slack memory is disabled by default, because it in-
creases the chance of a task being killed, but even so, 10%
of LS tasks override this, and 79% of batch tasks do so be-
cause it’s a default setting of the MapReduce framework.
This complements the results for reclaimed resources (§5.5).
Batch tasks are willing to exploit unused as well as reclaimed
memory opportunistically: most of the time this works, al-
though the occasional batch task is sacriﬁced when an LS
task needs resources in a hurry.
7.
Related work
Resource scheduling has been studied for decades, in con-
texts as varied as wide-area HPC supercomputing Grids, net-
works of workstations, and large-scale server clusters. We
focus here on only the most relevant work in the context of
large-scale server clusters.
Several recent studies have analyzed cluster traces from
Yahoo!, Google, and Facebook [20, 52, 63, 68, 70, 80, 82],
and illustrate the challenges of scale and heterogeneity in-
herent in these modern datacenters and workloads. [69] con-
tains a taxonomy of cluster manager architectures.
Apache Mesos [45] splits the resource management and
placement functions between a central resource manager
(somewhat like Borgmaster minus its scheduler) and mul-
tiple “frameworks” such as Hadoop [41] and Spark [73]
using an offer-based mechanism. Borg mostly centralizes
these functions using a request-based mechanism that scales
quite well. DRF [29, 35, 36, 66] was initially developed for
Mesos; Borg uses priorities and admission quotas instead.
The Mesos developers have announced ambitions to extend
Mesos to include speculative resource assignment and recla-
mation, and to ﬁx some of the issues identiﬁed in [69].
YARN [76] is a Hadoop-centric cluster manager. Each ap-
plication has a manager that negotiates for the resources it
needs with a central resource manager; this is much the same
scheme that Google MapReduce jobs have used to obtain
resources from Borg since about 2008. YARN’s resource
manager only recently became fault tolerant. A related open-
source effort is the Hadoop Capacity Scheduler [42] which
provides multi-tenant support with capacity guarantees, hi-
erarchical queues, elastic sharing and fairness. YARN has re-
cently been extended to support multiple resource types, pri-
orities, preemptions, and advanced admission control [21].
The Tetris research prototype [40] supports makespan-aware
job packing.
Facebook’s Tupperware [64], is a Borg-like system for
scheduling cgroup containers on a cluster; only a few details
have been disclosed, although it seems to provide a form
of resource reclamation. Twitter has open-sourced Aurora
[5], a Borg-like scheduler for long running services that runs
on top of Mesos, with a conﬁguration language and state
machine similar to Borg’s.
The Autopilot system from Microsoft [48] provides “au-
tomating software provisioning and deployment; system
monitoring; and carrying out repair actions to deal with
faulty software and hardware” for Microsoft clusters. The
Borg ecosystem provides similar features, but space pre-
cludes a discussion here; Isaard [48] outlines many best
practices that we adhere to as well.
Quincy [49] uses a network ﬂow model to provide fairness-
and data locality-aware scheduling for data-processing DAGs
on clusters of a few hundred nodes. Borg uses quota and pri-
orities to share resources among users and scales to tens of
thousands of machines. Quincy handles execution graphs
directly while this is built separately on top of Borg.
Cosmos [44] focuses on batch processing, with an em-
phasis on ensuring that its users get fair access to resources
they have donated to the cluster. It uses a per-job manager to
acquire resources; few details are publicly available.
Microsoft’s Apollo system [13] uses per-job schedulers
for short-lived batch jobs to achieve high throughput on clus-
ters that seem to be comparably-sized to Borg cells. Apollo
uses opportunistic execution of lower-priority background
work to boost utilization to high levels at the cost of (some-
times) multi-day queueing delays. Apollo nodes provide a
prediction matrix of starting times for tasks as a function
of size over two resource dimensions, which the schedulers
combine with estimates of startup costs and remote-data-
access to make placement decisions, modulated by random
delays to reduce collisions. Borg uses a central scheduler for
placement decisions based on state about prior allocations,
can handle more resource dimensions, and focuses on the
needs of high-availability, long-running applications; Apollo
can probably handle a higher task arrival rate.
Alibaba’s Fuxi [84] supports data-analysis workloads;
it has been running since 2009. Like Borgmaster, a cen-
tral FuxiMaster (replicated for failure-tolerance) gathers
resource-availability information from nodes, accepts re-
quests from applications, and matches one to the other. The
Fuxi incremental scheduling policy is the inverse of Borg’s
equivalence classes: instead of matching each task to one
of a suitable set of machines, Fuxi matches newly-available
resources against a backlog of pending work. Like Mesos,
Fuxi allows “virtual resource” types to be deﬁned. Only syn-
thetic workload results are publicly available.
Omega [69] supports multiple parallel, specialized “verti-
cals” that are each roughly equivalent to a Borgmaster minus
its persistent store and link shards. Omega schedulers use
optimistic concurrency control to manipulate a shared repre-
sentation of desired and observed cell state stored in a cen-
tral persistent store, which is synced to/from the Borglets by
a separate link component. The Omega architecture was de-
signed to support multiple distinct workloads that have their


=== PDF page 13 ===
own application-speciﬁc RPC interface, state machines, and
scheduling policies (e.g., long-running servers, batch jobs
from various frameworks, infrastructure services like clus-
ter storage systems, virtual machines from the Google Cloud
Platform). On the other hand, Borg offers a “one size ﬁts all”
RPC interface, state machine semantics, and scheduler pol-
icy, which have grown in size and complexity over time as a
result of needing to support many disparate workloads, and
scalability has not yet been a problem (§3.4).
Google’s open-source Kubernetes system [53] places
applications in Docker containers [28] onto multiple host
nodes. It runs both on bare metal (like Borg) and on various
cloud hosting providers, such as Google Compute Engine.
It is under active development by many of the same engi-
neers who built Borg. Google offers a hosted version called
Google Container Engine [39]. We discuss how lessons from
Borg are being applied to Kubernetes in the next section.
The high-performance computing community has a long
tradition of work in this area (e.g., Maui, Moab, Platform
LSF [2, 47, 50]); however the requirements of scale, work-
loads and fault tolerance are different from those of Google’s
cells. In general, such systems achieve high utilization by
having large backlogs (queues) of pending work.
Virtualization providers such as VMware [77] and data-
center solution providers such as HP and IBM [46] provide
cluster management solutions that typically scale to O(1000)
machines. In addition, several research groups have proto-
typed systems that improve the quality of scheduling deci-
sions in certain ways (e.g., [25, 40, 72, 74]).
And ﬁnally, as we have indicated, another important part
of managing large scale clusters is automation and “operator
scaleout”. [43] describes how planning for failures, multi-
tenancy, health checking, admission control, and restartabil-
ity are necessary to achieve high numbers of machines per
operator. Borg’s design philosophy is similar and allows us
to support tens of thousands of machines per operator (SRE).
8.
Lessons and future work
In this section we recount some of the qualitative lessons
we’ve learned from operating Borg in production for more
than a decade, and describe how these observations have
been leveraged in designing Kubernetes [53].
8.1
Lessons learned: the bad
We begin with some features of Borg that serve as cautionary
tales, and informed alternative designs in Kubernetes.
Jobs are restrictive as the only grouping mechanism
for tasks. Borg has no ﬁrst-class way to manage an entire
multi-job service as a single entity, or to refer to related
instances of a service (e.g., canary and production tracks).
As a hack, users encode their service topology in the job
name and build higher-level management tools to parse these
names. At the other end of the spectrum, it’s not possible to
refer to arbitrary subsets of a job, which leads to problems
like inﬂexible semantics for rolling updates and job resizing.
To avoid such difﬁculties, Kubernetes rejects the job no-
tion and instead organizes its scheduling units (pods) using
labels – arbitrary key/value pairs that users can attach to any
object in the system. The equivalent of a Borg job can be
achieved by attaching a job:jobname label to a set of pods,
but any other useful grouping can be represented too, such
as the service, tier, or release-type (e.g., production, stag-
ing, test). Operations in Kubernetes identify their targets by
means of a label query that selects the objects that the op-
eration should apply to. This approach gives more ﬂexibility
than the single ﬁxed grouping of a job.
One IP address per machine complicates things. In
Borg, all tasks on a machine use the single IP address of
their host, and thus share the host’s port space. This causes
a number of difﬁculties: Borg must schedule ports as a re-
source; tasks must pre-declare how many ports they need,
and be willing to be told which ones to use when they start;
the Borglet must enforce port isolation; and the naming and
RPC systems must handle ports as well as IP addresses.
Thanks to the advent of Linux namespaces, VMs, IPv6,
and software-deﬁned networking, Kubernetes can take a
more user-friendly approach that eliminates these complica-
tions: every pod and service gets its own IP address, allowing
developers to choose ports rather than requiring their soft-
ware to adapt to the ones chosen by the infrastructure, and
removes the infrastructure complexity of managing ports.
Optimizing for power users at the expense of casual
ones. Borg provides a large set of features aimed at “power
users” so they can ﬁne-tune the way their programs are run
(the BCL speciﬁcation lists about 230 parameters): the ini-
tial focus was supporting the largest resource consumers at
Google, for whom efﬁciency gains were paramount. Unfor-
tunately the richness of this API makes things harder for the
“casual” user, and constrains its evolution. Our solution has
been to build automation tools and services that run on top of
Borg, and determine appropriate settings from experimenta-
tion. These beneﬁt from the freedom to experiment afforded
by failure-tolerant applications: if the automation makes a
mistake it is a nuisance, not a disaster.
8.2
Lessons learned: the good
On the other hand, a number of Borg’s design features have
been remarkably beneﬁcial and have stood the test of time.
Allocs are useful. The Borg alloc abstraction spawned
the widely-used logsaver pattern (§2.4) and another popular
one in which a simple data-loader task periodically updates
the data used by a web server. Allocs and packages allow
such helper services to be developed by separate teams. The
Kubernetes equivalent of an alloc is the pod, which is a
resource envelope for one or more containers that are always
scheduled onto the same machine and can share resources.
Kubernetes uses helper containers in the same pod instead
of tasks in an alloc, but the idea is the same.


=== PDF page 14 ===
Cluster management is more than task management.
Although Borg’s primary role is to manage the lifecycles
of tasks and machines, the applications that run on Borg
beneﬁt from many other cluster services, including naming
and load balancing. Kubernetes supports naming and load
balancing using the service abstraction: a service has a name
and a dynamic set of pods deﬁned by a label selector. Any
container in the cluster can connect to the service using the
service name. Under the covers, Kubernetes automatically
load-balances connections to the service among the pods that
match the label selector, and keeps track of where the pods
are running as they get rescheduled over time due to failures.
Introspection is vital. Although Borg almost always
“just works,” when something goes wrong, ﬁnding the root
cause can be challenging. An important design decision in
Borg was to surface debugging information to all users rather
than hiding it: Borg has thousands of users, so “self-help”
has to be the ﬁrst step in debugging. Although this makes it
harder for us to deprecate features and change internal poli-
cies that users come to rely on, it is still a win, and we’ve
found no realistic alternative. To handle the enormous vol-
ume of data, we provide several levels of UI and debugging
tools, so users can quickly identify anomalous events related
to their jobs, and then drill down to detailed event and error
logs from their applications and the infrastructure itself.
Kubernetes aims to replicate many of Borg’s introspec-
tion techniques. For example, it ships with tools such as
cAdvisor [15] for resource monitoring, and log aggregation
based on Elasticsearch/Kibana [30] and Fluentd [32]. The
master can be queried for a snapshot of its objects’ state.
Kubernetes has a uniﬁed mechanism that all components can
use to record events (e.g., a pod being scheduled, a container
failing) that are made available to clients.
The master is the kernel of a distributed system.
Borgmaster was originally designed as a monolithic sys-
tem, but over time, it became more of a kernel sitting at the
heart of an ecosystem of services that cooperate to man-
age user jobs. For example, we split off the scheduler and
the primary UI (Sigma) into separate processes, and added
services for admission control, vertical and horizontal auto-
scaling, re-packing tasks, periodic job submission (cron),
workﬂow management, and archiving system actions for
off-line querying. Together, these have allowed us to scale
up the workload and feature set without sacriﬁcing perfor-
mance or maintainability.
The Kubernetes architecture goes further: it has an API
server at its core that is responsible only for processing re-
quests and manipulating the underlying state objects. The
cluster management logic is built as small, composable
micro-services that are clients of this API server, such as
the replication controller, which maintains the desired num-
ber of replicas of a pod in the face of failures, and the node
controller, which manages the machine lifecycle.
8.3
Conclusion
Virtually all of Google’s cluster workloads have switched to
use Borg over the past decade. We continue to evolve it, and
have applied the lessons we learned from it to Kubernetes.

After the camera-ready copy was finalized, we noticed a few inadvertent omissions and

The user perspective 
SREs do much more than system administration: they are the engineers responsible for Google’s 
production services.  They design and implement software, including automation systems, and 
manage applications, service infrastructure and platforms to ensure high performance and 
reliability at Google scale. 
Related work 
Borg leveraged much from its internal predecessor, the Global Work Queue system, which was 
initially developed by Jeff Dean, Olcan Sercinoglu, and Percy Liang. 
 
Condor [1] has been widely used for aggregating collections of idle resources, and its ClassAds 
mechanism [2] supports declarative statements and automated attribute/property matching.

这些是相关知识链的质量标准，不是每份文件必须照抄的六个标题。前置知识可以链接，但本章承担的核心算法、推导与边界不能用链接或名词清单代替。数学定义与真实硬件限制可以确定；某个引擎采用的分层、布局、算法和优化顺序应作为带前提的选择解释。

## 正文与算法

正文以问题和机制展开：说明问题为什么出现，定义对象和合法性，展开算法、数据流与状态更新，推导成本与组合关系，用设定算例、反例和区分实验解释结论如何改变。篇幅与结构由内容决定，不规定候选数、反例数或统一段落数量。

实现逻辑可以转写为完整的算法伪代码，使用 pseudocode 标记的代码块。伪代码应给出输入输出、初始化、循环/分支、更新顺序和完成条件；正文说明正确性不变量、特殊输入与成本。调用一个未解释的库函数不能代替算法。现成 kernel、项目类结构、注册器、兼容分支和可执行命令保留在工程中。

公式须说明符号、单位、轴和假设。区分逻辑数据量、实际设备事务量、容量峰值和关键路径时间；重叠工作不能把全部耗时直接相加。模型结构、数值策略、硬件能力或运行规模改变后，重新检查依赖与成本。

## 来源阅读链

论文保留直接可读的原始 PDF、必要图片和出处；来源说明用自己的话展开算法、推导、论文结论及其条件，明确哪些是论文报告、哪些是本库计算。文档同样保留原文，提炼定义、语义、约束及其设计含义。

源码可以供知识编写者核对机制。交给 Agent 的内容应是经过核对的算法伪代码、数据流、状态关系与条件化事实，不能把整个实现文件称作知识原文。文档/源码混合资料按实际内容选择可读文档；文件扩展名、压缩包形式和仓库名称本身不决定知识价值。已有源码归档可以保留供溯源审计，其字节和哈希不因来源说明修订而改变。

正文引用需要带实质内容，再指向来源说明；来源说明指向可读论文或文档。必要内容离线可读，不依赖 Agent 联网补全。准确版本留作证据身份；只有影响本题合法性或成本的版本事实进入论证，不搬运与本题无关的参数和分支。

## 逐层阅读

阅读入口按主题地图、章节摘要与问题/前提、二级节结构、完整论证、来源原文展开。Agent 自主选择阅读深度；索引与检索结果提供相邻机制，不产生必读清单。读取按实际字符范围与冻结修订记录；读过摘要不等于读过整章。

## Base、观测和 workflow

Base 的来源事实受发布版本的时间上限约束；编辑日期不改变事实日期。新的整理和独立推导保留真实日期与依据，后续实验不能伪装成历史 seed。

运行观测保存环境、workload、测量方法、数值/单位/不确定性、实验证据与真实日期。机制知识解释因果、条件、预测和反例。Workflow 保存一类局部设计、诊断或验证问题的触发条件、前提、步骤、检查与退出/调整条件、成本和复用边界。三者相互引用，不能用一次成功代替机制解释或跨条件验证。

Evolution 提炼、Diagnostician 独立复核，沿已有发布和证据机制进入后续冻结、检索与读取。Workflow 为可选方法，不自动成为 Controller 的全局顺序。跨任务资格使用现有权威晋升机制，负面与不确定结果保留，不建立平行资格体系。

## 修订、覆盖和验证

已有技术对象优先深化原章；独立对象才新增章节。修订保存登记前正文与元数据的准确字节，更新 catalog、来源说明哈希、导航、时间审计、VERSION 与变更清单。已存在的来源归档保持原身份。

覆盖审计同时检查能力域、具体算法与跨机制组合，区分完整解释、仅提及、缺少推导、缺少证据和缺失；篇数和术语命中不是覆盖证明。结构/身份检查、独立算法算例、运行时读取/发布测试与真实构建效果分别报告。通过前几项不能声称已证明知识改善了 Agent 的系统设计或性能。

六项标准的具体追问、组合案例、来源核对和使用效果边界见[知识内容审查](knowledge-review.md)。[Attention 模块](attention-module.md)是内容深度的已完成样例；其算法、硬件映射与组合状态按主题选择展开，不规定所有专题复制同样的结构。逐篇扩展状态见[扩展状态](expansion-status.json)，导航登记不代表深度验收完成。

连续构建按[知识库构建 workflow](knowledge-build-workflow.md)执行：保存当前基线、分配专题、独立审查、真实检查、修订和统一登记；全库队列保留未完成项。固定的是输入、交付物与证据边界，内容是否充分仍需针对当前论证判断。

## 知识库承担什么任务

本库支持 InfraAgents 根据模型、workload、硬件和服务目标，从空工程构建、检验与持续优化完整推理系统。知识应提供五种帮助：还原问题的理论基础；区分合法条件与可探索的设计空间；给出足以独立实现的算法与状态关系；支持成本预测、实验和诊断；保存能够被反驳、修正和迁移的经验。

一条有用的阅读链应支持读者形成这样的推理：任务与输入条件 → 正确性要求 → 候选算法与数据流 → 成本预测 → 区分实验 → 实现结果 → 修正后的结论。某一章可以承担其中一部分，但承担核心算法的地方不能只列注意事项或把关键步骤交给源码。

## 六项标准怎样落实到实际问题

| 内容标准 | 审阅时实际追问 | 过去发现的问题及其含义 |
|---|---|---|
| 原因、数学定义、输入输出和状态 | 为什么需要这个机制？每个量的轴、单位、范围和身份是什么？状态代表已知、已算、已确认还是已分配？ | FP8 只写“使用块尺度”不足以恢复分数和 PV 的共同单位；调度中的 token 已生成不等于其 KV 已计算 |
| 合法性与方案选择 | 哪条性质来自函数、数值契约或设备语义，哪条来自某个方案？等价性在实数、浮点还是特定误差范围内成立？ | 精确算术的归约结合性不能直接变成浮点逐位相同；图地址稳定不证明数据身份仍正确；内部 fragment 未公开就不能猜 lane 映射 |
| 算法、数据流和状态变化 | 能否写出初始化、推进、提交和结束？第一块、最后一块、空输入和失败分支怎样处理？每个被消费的量从哪里产生？ | 量化流程需要量化与恢复尺度；缓冲需要生产者、所有消费者及代次；硬件专题需要一条从逻辑 tile 到地址、线程、片上布局、指令输入和写回的完整路径 |
| 六类成本 | 是否在同一候选、相同输入和相同时间范围中列账？哪些量可以相加，哪些受关键路径和共享资源限制？ | 唯一 KV、各 head 请求流量和 DRAM 事务不能混算；共享容量只计一次；预留池与其中存活对象不能重复相加；深流水的驻留和 spill 会改变本来用于估时的吞吐 |

这些问题由主题决定使用范围。调度章节需要把就绪性、预算和输出归属连起来；缓存章节需要贯通身份、复制、发布和回收；硬件章节需要贯通布局、执行契约和资源。协议、统计或模型语义章节不必凭空增加矩阵指令实例。

## 从单个机制走到组合案例

分开解释各个机制之后，选择会改变合法性或成本的真实交界，追踪一次完整变化。例如共享前缀和私有尾块在追加、封存、发布、消费与回收期间，内容、scale、页表和读者必须属于一致的状态；调度器选中的工作必须已有上游输入和容量，而执行视图的压紧不能改变请求归属。

审阅者沿一次轨迹检查：发生了什么输入事件；哪些对象仍存活；谁能写；谁已经取得读取权；何时对消费者可见；失败后哪些旧状态仍有效；取消后哪些工作仍在途；何时能把同一物理资源交给下一使用者。对象需要身份或代次时，解释防止的具体错误。只有单次同步执行的算法不必引入多代次协议。

交界还包括“看似已经完成，下一步却没有输入”的状态。本轮调度审阅发现：完整命中 KV 而没有末行 logits 时，只按已知长度减 KV 长度选择工作会得到零，无法生成第一个新 token。修订明确了安全重算最后一个已知 token 的路径及共享写区隔离。沿状态图检查是否存在有合法请求却无后继事件的停滞，比只检查各状态的字段范围更有用。

组合案例应使读者能计算至少一项会影响决定的代价，并解释另一种选择何时反转。重点是让独立机制能够正确拼接，不是枚举所有组合。示例的页长、tile、队列策略和版本字段均为可替换选择。

## 阅读链与事实核对

先检查正文承担的核心知识，再检查直接来源说明与足以支持关键事实的固定论文或文档。保留原始资料的错误、版本身份和字节，在解释中纠正公式或限定结论；自己的推导不能归为论文实测。源码可以用于作者核对，但读者独立实现所需的事实应进入允许读取的算法说明。

审查记录写明读过哪些正文、哪些来源及其范围、发现的具体问题、实际修改与检查。只有读取摘要、术语检索或运行链接检查的专题，继续保留深度复核待完成状态。没有必要为了一个确定问题递归阅读所有引用。

## 内容与使用效果分别验收

内容审查判断六项标准在声明范围内是否有充分解释。作者侧算例验证代数、布局、边界、协议或成本模型；它需要独立参考、不变量或能触发错误的负对照，不能只让测试复述实现。读取测试检查冻结内容能否被取回及身份是否匹配。这三类证据各自有效，不能互相代替。

直接使用检验让 Agent 在没有现成实现的情况下处理正文未直接演示的问题：重新推导合法算法，改变输入或硬件条件后重算，面对错误提出竞争解释，收到反证后修改方案。保存允许资料、任务、模型/上下文、预算、答卷或实现、执行结果及失败归因。交叉审阅兼做推导练习可以发现内容缺口，但有共同上下文、作者经验或未隔离的环境时，只能声称完成这次练习。

如果要声称“知识改善了 Agent 的构建能力”，还需可比的知识版本或对照条件、多个代表任务以及预先说明的判断方法。目标 GPU 的数值、同步、重叠和性能仍需设备结果。没有最佳 tile 或流水级数不构成知识缺陷；没有解释如何推导候选、识别限制、测量与修正，才是内容缺口。

## 怎样给出审查结论

对每个问题给出正文位置、明确结论与证据边界，区分“已完整解释”“仅提及”“缺推导”“缺证据”“缺失”。这些描述可按实际内容组合使用，不转成总分或用测试数量抵消关键算法缺口。

已经修复的问题在新修订中复核后关闭，不沿用旧审查中“仍缺 FP8/硬件映射/组合案例”的判断。新的缺口必须来自当前字节。Attention 当前的两个具体案例已补足内容展开，实际 Agent 独立构建与目标 GPU 效果仍有各自的验证边界。以当前内容和当前证据决定结论，不为了持续审查而不断增加验收条件。

扩展工作优先完成相关专题的一条知识链，再复核跨专题衔接。当前批次与逐篇状态见[扩展状态](expansion-status.json)；历史审查保留当时结论，不覆盖成当前状态。

扩容的效果从新实例真正就绪时开始。控制面希望得到几个副本、已经分配几个设备、已经启动几个进程，以及有多少容量能够接收合格请求，属于不同状态。弹性策略需要在负载变化与这些状态之间建立反馈。

## 将启动延迟放进请求时间轴

一个新实例需要取得资源、获取制品、加载转换、建立通信组、编译/预热和加入路由。已有本地权重、CPU 缓存或编译缓存会改变关键路径；同时启动大量副本又会争用共享存储和网络。[ServerlessLLM](../sources/S-SERVERLESSLLM.md) 将多级加载、局部性和启动时间共同调度，其机制支持比较冷热路径，不证明扩容数量与服务能力即时成比例。

队列长度也不等于待执行时间。长提示、长输出、不同模型和缓存命中让每个请求的工作量不同。可按阶段估算剩余工作和 deadline，再用实际就绪容量校准。只以 GPU 利用率触发扩容，会漏掉 CPU 分词、网络背压或加载 I/O 饱和；此时增加 GPU 实例可能继续放大原瓶颈。

在固定服务率的简化模型中，未就绪阶段的积压增长为到达率减去现有服务率的正部。真实自回归服务还需跟踪 KV 占用、输出增长和 prefill/decode 的相互干扰，不能用这一标量模型代替准入检查。

## 三条弹性路线

常驻容量直接吸收突发，支付空闲驻留成本。保留热备用或分层缓存能减少启动时间，但仍占 CPU 内存、SSD、设备或预热资源。完全按需启动释放更多闲置容量，却依赖突发可预测性、较宽松的首 token 目标或明确的拒绝策略。

扩容应考虑实例对数据路径的新增负载：增加 decode 实例可能争用同一 KV 池，增加 prefill 实例可能争用权重加载和互连。多模型放置还决定扩给哪个版本以及是否挤走另一个租户的热状态。相同数量的实例在不同拓扑或 quota 下，不保证相同服务率。

滞回和最短驻留时间用于解决具体的测量延迟与反复启停：短时队列下降不能立即回收仍在预热的实例，短尖峰也未必值得启动一个几十秒后才有用的副本。阈值由启动、排空、计费粒度和负载变化共同决定，不应把任意固定阈值当作跨任务常数。

## 可复算的突发算例

设定当前两实例各稳定处理 20 请求/s，突然到达 70 请求/s，扩容一个实例需要 20 s，突发持续 10 s。若没有拒绝或其他瓶颈，前 10 s 积压 300 请求；之后到达率恢复 20 请求/s，旧容量 40 请求/s 用额外 20 请求/s 消化积压，因此第 20 s 新实例就绪时仍有 100 个请求排队。新容量 60 请求/s 在持续 20 请求/s 到达下，还需 2.5 s 清空。

这只是一组流体近似，不能证明个体尾延迟达标。若要求请求 1 s 内开始服务，该次反应式扩容远晚于多数突发请求的 deadline。热备用、预测性加载或明确拒绝才可能改变这个窗口。若突发持续 60 s，只新增一个实例仍只有 60 请求/s，低于 70 请求/s，到达积压会继续增长；“已经扩了一台”不是稳定性结论。

另设每实例需要从共享存储读取 12 GiB，四个冷启动共享 6 GiB/s 的有效出口。无其他流量时，总读取至少 8 s；不能为四个实例分别使用独占时的 2 s 估计。节点缓存减少出口字节，但仍需计算本地读、CPU 转换与设备复制。

## 缩容和滚动更新

缩容先撤销新请求准入，再等待已有请求结束，或迁移到有容量且版本相容的目标。长流式请求、慢客户端和工具等待会延长排空；若设置最长排空时间，超时后的终止或可恢复重试必须进入服务协议。当前连接数降到零也不能证明设备传输和最后一次执行已经完成。

更新模型版本与缩容组合时，先保证新版本就绪，再改变新请求绑定；旧请求仍按旧版本完成。容量冗余应包含“一个实例正在更新，同时另一个故障”的实际要求。没有故障后余量，就不能把正常时的满利用率当成可用性证明。

## 验证与反转条件

重放负载时保留真实时间和突发相关性，逐时刻记录 offered/拒绝/完成请求、已就绪容量、队列、加载阶段和资源争用。注入资源申请失败、制品缺片、预热失败、路由迟到、缩容中断及状态迁移失败，检查请求只由一个有效代次提交，失败实例不会被算入容量。

分别比较常驻、热备用与按需启动的合格完成数、尾延迟、设备占用时间和制品流量。短而不可预测的突发、严格首 token 约束通常要求更多即时容量；长且可预测的负载变化、昂贵的闲置资源更支持动态调整。最终选择要和[成本能耗](cost-and-energy.md)的统计边界保持一致。

# K-SYS-011：模型生命周期：加载、就绪、排空与版本切换

模型服务的版本是一组共同定义输入到输出函数的制品和执行约束。权重、配置、tokenizer/processor、adapter、量化参数以及执行布局必须在同一次请求中保持相容。生命周期管理解决的不是单纯启动或停止进程，而是三个问题：何时有资格接收请求；切流后谁继续履行旧请求；何时能够把旧资源交给另一个版本。

文件存在、端口能连接、加载调用返回和路由已经更新，分别只证明一部分工作完成。把这些事件混成一个 ready 标志，会使未完成的执行组接收请求，或让旧请求读取已经被覆盖的权重。

## 版本、实例和就绪范围

区分三个身份。

- 制品身份 v：固定清单所引用的权重、配置、processor、adapter、量化与必要布局依赖。读取清单后固定其版本，不能逐片重新解析 latest。
- 加载实例 g：一次具体加载及其执行组。相同 v 的重试也创建新 g；旧尝试的完成通知不能使新尝试就绪。
- 路由代次 e：一次准入配置的身份。即使别名经历 v1→v2→v1，e 仍递增，防止第一次 v1 的过期路由重新有效。

实例内还要保存逻辑 rank 到实际设备、设备资源与地址绑定的映射。容器里的 device 0 不是稳定物理身份；设备重建、MIG 配置或执行组改变后，需要重新验证相应依赖。[部署环境](deployment-environment.md)解释设备暴露与真实资源边界。

将请求 r 的一次合法执行写为

(y,S′)=F_v(x,S;θ_r)，

其中 x 是已经按该版本解释的输入，S 是 KV、递归状态、RNG、grammar 等请求状态，θ_r 是采样与执行选项，y 是本次产生的结果。生命周期输出除了 y，还包括请求的绑定 (r,v,g)、准入票据、状态归属与最后使用责任。processor 参与输入解释，因此不能先用可变别名对应的 tokenizer 编码，再随意绑定另一个版本。可以先固定版本并持有其责任后处理输入，也可以在正式准入时验证输入解释身份一致。

就绪证书可描述为

C_g=(v,g,E_g,P_g,Ω_g,Π_g)，

E_g 是环境和执行依赖身份，P_g 是完整 rank/设备/布局计划，Ω_g 是允许公开的请求范围，Π_g 是制品检查、完成证据和代表路径验证记录。Ω_g 应能判定模型、dtype、输入几何、上下文上限、adapter 路径、图桶或受验证回退路径是否合法。代表输入通过是该路径的证据，不是整个 Ω_g 的数值正确性证明；范围的推广还要依靠形状 guard、容量边界和执行契约。

就绪资格与瞬时可接收容量分开。C_g 仍有效，但 KV 满了，可以暂时拒绝或排队；一个 rank 或设备依赖失效，则撤销相关资格。不能把暂时过载变成反复重启，也不能把历史预热成功当作失效环境仍然有效的证明。

## 从制品到就绪的准备算法

采用 PREPARING、READY、OPEN、DRAINING、RETIRING、RETIRED，以及失败状态 FAILED。READY 的新准入门仍关闭；OPEN 表示可按当前路由取得新准入；DRAINING 允许已有请求继续，却不允许新请求绑定。状态名称可以合并，以下完成条件不能合并。

```pseudocode
输入：不可变清单 v；不复用的实例身份 g；执行计划 P；公开范围 Ω；资源预算
输出：未发布的就绪实例 C_g，或带明确阶段与未结责任的失败结果

1. 创建 PREPARING(g)，关闭准入门；初始化 rank 完成集合为空。
2. 固定清单与全部依赖身份；检查必要分片、长度、完整性、张量关系、
   processor、adapter 和量化/布局元数据。发现缺片或不相容则转失败。
3. 按每个设备和主机统计准备期间的唯一存储并集与预留。
   同时计入仍存活的旧版本、转换区、图池、通信区和预热状态。
   取得全部必要资源的预留；任一处不足则等待、调整计划或失败。
4. 对每个 rank，按 P 加载并转换完整张量，建立真实设备与布局映射。
   每次异步访问在提交前登记使用责任；源与目的地址受保护到最后访问结束。
5. 建立完整执行组及所需通信上下文；共同核对 v、g、P 和操作协议。
6. 为实际公开的执行变体建立或核对编译产物、图及工作区。
   复用 key 包含其真实依赖，不以模型名称单独判断命中。
7. 在实际执行线程设定模型评估行为和所需推理上下文。
   运行代表路径、边界与独立参考比较；检查必要 rank 的共同结果。
   预热的 KV、RNG、输出与测试请求使用隔离状态。
8. 等待影响执行可读性的加载、转换和初始化完成证据。
   清理或隔离预热状态；不能把测试请求历史交给正式请求。
9. 每个 rank 仅为当前 (v,g,P,Ω) 报告完成；重复或旧尝试报告不改变资格。
   只有全部必要 rank、依赖和验证条件满足，才发布 C_g 并进入 READY。
10. 任一步失败：关闭准入，记录最早失败与已完成范围，进入 FAILED。
    停止后续准备，排空已提交访问，解除绑定后释放可回收资源。
    超时只记录未结责任；重试使用新的 g，不复活这个失败尝试。
```

第 3 步需要逐设备判断。两个 rank 总需求小于两张卡的总容量，不保证某个 rank 的局部峰值可行。设备插件的 time-slicing 份额也不会创造额外显存或独立故障域；固定 v0.16.1 的共享资源声明只能支持相应访问与限额契约，不能代替这里的容量检查。

第 7 步同时涉及模型行为与运行簿记。[S-TORCH-INFERENCE](../sources/S-TORCH-INFERENCE.md) 的机制说明指出 inference_mode 是线程局部状态，不会自动调用 eval。入口线程进入推理模式，不证明后台执行线程相同；关闭 autograd 也不证明 Dropout、统计 buffer 或其他可变模型状态已经符合服务契约。

编译产物的失效范围由依赖决定。权重作为运行时参数、ABI 和布局保持相容时，数值替换不一定要求重编译；常量折叠、预打包格式或捕获地址改变时，则要重建受影响产物。无论是否复用编译代码，旧图仍引用的地址都不能被原地覆盖。详见[编译与动态形状](../frameworks/compile-dynamic-shapes.md)和[CUDA Graph](../frameworks/cuda-graph-buffers.md)。

## 准入与切流必须有共同排序点

定义权威路由 A=(e,g)，并为实例保存准入门。下面选择一个保守模型：路由变更、门控和请求责任登记在同一串行状态域中排序，设备资源由该域可核对的预留账保证。它说明需要的原子关系，不要求把所有设备工作放进一个锁。

```pseudocode
准入(r, 请求摘要, 期望路由 e/g, 请求范围 σ)：
  在权威状态域中：
    若 r 已有准入记录：
      同身份与摘要的重试返回已有记录；冲突输入拒绝。
    核对当前 A=(e,g)，实例为 OPEN，C_g 有效，σ 属于 Ω_g。
    核对输入解释身份与 v 一致。
    计算本请求所需的逐设备增量预留 δ，包括已承诺的在途增长上界。
    若资源不足，按既定策略返回等待或拒绝，不创建半份正式请求。
    原子取得预留，登记逻辑请求责任 R_g 中的 r，
      写入不可变绑定 (r,v,g) 与准入票据，再返回接受。

切流(op, 期望代次 e, 目标 h)：
  在同一权威状态域中：
    若 op 已有决定，核对参数一致并返回原决定。
    核对路由代次仍为 e。
    核对 h 为 READY，或为尚未进入 RETIRING 且重新验证合格的 DRAINING；
      C_h、分配和环境依赖仍有效。
    关闭旧目标 g 的新准入门，令其进入 DRAINING。
    打开 h 的新准入门，令其进入 OPEN。
    原子写入 A=(e+1,h) 和 op 的已提交决定。
    保留全部已接受请求的原绑定和预留。
```

准入先发生，旧请求已经在 R_g 中，即使队列消息在切流后才抵达 worker，仍由 g 履行。切流先发生，拿着旧 e/g 的新准入必须被拒绝或重新解析路由。不能先在路由器读取 g，再在另一处无条件递增引用计数；两步之间可能完成排空和卸载。

缓存路由只用于提出候选，不能自行签发旧版本的新准入。若使用分散式租约代替共同权威域，需要另行给出签发、撤销、租约存活与排空之间的证明；单纯等待一个估计的缓存传播时间不足以完成这个证明。多控制节点也不能各自根据本地超时开放实例。

跨节点预留若需多步完成，先取得临时预留，全部成功并重新核对路由后才安装正式准入。未提交预留失败时撤销；已经发出的设备访问继续承担排空责任。上述原子步骤不能直接推断任意远程 allocator 天然具有跨节点事务。

切流确认丢失时，控制者查询 op 的权威决定；相同 op 的重试返回原结果。结果未知时保留原资源责任，不能根据本地超时反向切流。回退是另一项有新 op 和新 e 的切流：它改变后续准入，不能撤回已经交付的回答，也不能重新绑定 v2 的活跃请求。

若旧实例仍完整驻留、尚未 RETIRING 且资格重新验证有效，可以重新开放它。已经开始拆除图、通信组或权重的实例必须重新准备，不能仅把状态标签改成 OPEN。别名回到同一个 g，也不使早期 e 的票据重新有效。

## 排空、取消与卸载算法

对实例 g 分开记录四类责任：R_g 是仍可继续执行的逻辑请求；U_g 是已经登记的 kernel、复制、传输等实际访问票据；B_g 是图、注册区和执行对象的地址绑定；O_g 是仍借用实例资源的输出消费者。每张票据含实例身份、用途和不复用的操作身份。请求数为零不等于后三者为空。

```pseudocode
已有请求继续执行：
  核对正式准入票据与不可变 (r,v,g)，不重新读取当前别名。
  核对请求仍有效，实例没有进入 FAILED、RETIRING 或 RETIRED。
  在提交任何异步访问前，为其全部实际资源登记 U 票据。
  对必要 rank 提交相容计划；发生部分提交失败时停止受影响尝试，
    按执行组恢复契约处理，排空已经发出的操作。
  输出若借用资源，先登记 O 再交给消费者，不能留下无人保护的交接窗口。

请求结束或取消：
  关闭该请求的新业务提交与新执行入口；按协议确定其终态。
  解除 R 与可解除的逻辑预留。
  保留已有 U、B、O；取消通知和终态标签不充当物理完成证据。

开始拆除实例：
  核对新准入门关闭，实例不再是有效路由目标，R 为空。
  原子进入 RETIRING；从此拒绝新请求、重新开放和新的地址绑定。
  停止准备及后台产生新工作的入口。
  在相关重放结束后拆除图、注册与通信绑定，逐项结束 B。
  持续处理真实完成证据，逐项结束 U 和 O。
  完成通知必须匹配 (g,操作身份,受保护范围)；旧代或重复通知不修改新责任。
  U、B、O 全部结束后，销毁执行对象并归还资源，进入 RETIRED。

排空期限到达：
  对仍活跃请求执行预先声明的终止、恢复或合法迁移策略。
  不伪造成功完成，也不把期限到达当作设备停止。
  无法证明结束的资源保持隔离，列出具体责任及解除条件。
```

这里选择整实例保守拆除。实际可以在对象级分别回收：若输出已经复制到独立主存且不再借用权重或设备缓冲，它不必延长这些对象的生命期；但复制完成与消费者交接必须有明确证据。反过来，主机响应线程结束也不证明设备 DMA 已经完成。

逻辑请求在 DRAINING 中仍可执行，因而不能仅因准入门关闭便拒绝所有旧迭代。取消则关闭该请求未来工作，但不能让某个 rank 单独跳过其他 rank 已经参与的 collective。执行组错误与单请求业务终态必须分别处理，见[推理服务恢复](serving-recovery.md)及[取消与完成](cancellation-resource-completion.md)。

本状态机的安全条件是：全部访问提交入口受责任登记约束，完成证据真实覆盖最后使用，控制决定有共同排序，接收端核对准入与执行身份。它不自行实现分布式共识、持久日志或设备中止。控制记录丢失、worker 崩溃或故障域不明确时，需要相应恢复协议；本地引用计数不能独立证明远端访问已经结束。

## 三种切换路线及状态相容边界

停止旧服务、排空后加载新版本，峰值较低，但存在服务空窗。新旧并存后切流，可以在准备新版本时继续服务旧请求，代价是双版本及准备过程的容量和资源争用。滚动更换多个副本，把容量峰值和容量下降分到多步，却要求每一步的剩余合格容量都足够。以上是带前提的策略选择，不是三种不同正确性要求。

一次请求始终绑定原 v。adapter 更新也以新不可变对象发布；不能在旧地址原地覆写 A/B、scale 或描述符。相同 adapter 名称、相同 shape 和相同物理地址都不证明内容身份相同。KV 的相容身份要覆盖影响该状态的依赖闭包，默认把模型与 adapter 版本纳入其中，见[多 LoRA 服务](../algorithms/lora-serving.md)。

会话下一轮使用新版本是协议选择。可以保留原版本并支付驻留，也可以用新 processor 重新解释可重放输入、重新计算状态；不能默认把旧 KV 接到新权重后继续。若声称某类状态可跨版本保留，需要证明该状态的全部生成依赖与后继消费契约相容，而不是只比较张量尺寸。

迁移地点与切换模型版本也不同。ServerlessLLM §5 利用相同只读模型下的 token 重算来重建 KV，并让目标先处理前缀、最后处理源端新增 token。这支持特定 Transformer 状态恢复路线，不证明任意模型状态只靠 token 即可恢复。通用迁移仍需冻结共同恢复边界、保存 RNG/grammar/递归与输出状态，并只移交一份提交权。

设已知 token 为 x[0,n)，已有完整模型状态到 p，p≤n。已采样或已交付 token 不一定已有自己的 KV。重建应明确恢复到 p，还是合法推进到另一个边界，避免重复采样或遗漏末行 logits。目标 READY 只说明具备接管条件，不等于已取得业务提交权。完整迁移与确认丢失处理沿用[取消与完成](cancellation-resource-completion.md)中的授权协议，本章的路由切流不替代它。

## 启动、驻留和有效容量的条件化成本

启动时间取决于资源等待、取得制品、加载转换、执行组建立、编译与预热、路由生效之间的依赖。对任务图中事件 j，若前驱集合为 pred(j)，独立资源且没有额外争用时有

F_j=max_{i∈pred(j)}F_i+t_j。

F_j、t_j 的单位为秒；无前驱时以前置可开始时刻为边界。共享 SSD、NIC、CPU 或主存的任务还要加入资源顺序或有效能力约束。不能同时给每个任务独占带宽并声称它们完全重叠。

若各 rank 独立完成本地流水，资源排队 q_r 发生在其前，L_r 已包含本地加载、检查、编译与预热，则

T_ready=max_r(q_r+L_r)+T_group。

T_group 只计真正位于这些工作之后的共同验证或屏障；已包含在 L_r 中的事件不能再加。两个 rank 的本地工作均需 4 s，排队分别为 0、1 s，之后共同验证为 0.5 s，则准备完成为 5.5 s。路由安装及必要传播另计；过期路由被安全拒绝期间，实际可接收吞吐仍可能下降。

ServerlessLLM §6.2 用 q+n/b 估计特定加载路径，其中 n 为模型分片字节，b 为所用流水中的慢层带宽。该系统以每服务器顺序加载减轻争用。这个估计不能直接覆盖任意并发、编译、预热和分布式准备图，也不能把热缓存下的 b 外推为冷启动带宽。

六类费用应在同一次切换范围中核对。

| 成本 | 需要计入的机制与条件 |
|---|---|
| 计算 | 解包、转换、完整性检查、编译、预热和可能的状态重算；重算是完整模型工作，不只包含 Attention |
| 访存 | 文件读取、CPU 转换读写、H2D、图输入与状态初始化；逻辑有效字节不等于 SSD、主存或 HBM 实际事务 |
| 通信 | 制品分发、执行组初始化、预热 collective、迁移和控制记录；按链路及单 rank/全组口径分别计量 |
| 准备 | 清单解析、对象建立、资源预留、设备映射、编译缓存核对与图捕获；常驻一次和频繁切换的摊销不同 |
| 同步 | 生产到消费、组内共同完成、准入切流排序和失败排空；host 返回不代表设备完成，逻辑发布也不必等于全设备同步 |
| 驻留 | 新旧权重、KV、执行/图池、转换区、预热状态及未排空资源；按同一时刻的唯一物理存储计数 |

对设备 d，容量峰值为

M_d,peak=max_t Σ_{a∈A_d(t)} size(a)，

A_d(t) 是该时刻占用预算的唯一 backing 集合，包括完整池及池外分配。池内活跃对象是池的一部分，不能再与整个池重复相加；共享不可变页计一次，真实复制两份计两次。主机内存、设备内存和存储分别建账。allocator 的 allocated/reserved 是统计口径，不能未经覆盖关系核对便作为额外对象相加。

设设备可用 24 GiB，旧权重 12 GiB、旧请求 KV 5 GiB、共同运行与临时区 3 GiB。新权重另需 12 GiB，即使忽略新图和转换峰值，并存也需 32 GiB；排空旧 KV 后仍需 27 GiB。因此这组条件下单卡双版本并存不可行。可改用其他设备、降低满足数值契约的表示容量，或选择有空窗替换。提前报告就绪不会减少所需字节。

在完全串行的停止替换路径中，关闭准入到恢复服务的空窗可写成排空、回收、新准备与发布之和；若某些准备已经安全提前完成，则按依赖图重算，不能继续使用该串行和。并存路线虽然避免等待新版本准备才继续旧服务，却可能因加载抢占 PCIe、CPU 或主存而伤害旧请求延迟，需要与稳态执行共同测量。

排空墙钟时间由仍需履行的请求、访问、绑定与输出交接的最后依赖决定。若最后 kernel 和输出消费可以并行，不能将两者全部时长相加。取消后停止未来迭代可以减少设备工作，却不立即降低尚被保护的物理容量。

滚动策略还受服务率约束。设四个独立副本各能在声明负载下合格处理 20 请求/s，更新时一个副本排空，同时要求承受另一个副本故障，则剩余容量仅为 40 请求/s。到达 45 请求/s 时，正常更新的 60 请求/s 看似足够，故障后的要求却不成立。需要更多已就绪冗余、减小更新影响或明确降低服务承诺；尚在加载的副本不能计为 20 请求/s。

token 重算迁移可减少网络字节，但会增加目标计算与双端驻留。若传输 n 个 int64 token，主载荷为 8n 字节；KV 的逻辑主项若为 nτ 字节，τ 是每 token 的状态字节，则二者可相差很大。真正选择仍需比较目标模型准备、完整重算、最终增量和提交权移交。目标重算速率不高于源新增工作速率时，反复追赶不保证收敛，应冻结、降低源推进速度或放弃迁移。

# K-WORK-007：多模型放置：共同容量、混合执行与租户公平

多模型服务同时决定哪些版本驻留、各放在哪些设备、请求到达后去哪里，以及有限容量由哪些请求占有。完整权重不同的模型、共享基座的 adapters、同一模型的独立副本，具有不同的共享条件。模型名数量、逻辑资源份额和平均设备利用率都不能替代逐设备的容量与执行账。

放置的输入包括模型及版本、可用执行配置、设备与链路、请求到达和长度轨迹、租户份额、数值要求与服务目标。输出包括逐设备物理对象、模型副本及执行组、冷对象加载规则、请求绑定与准入决定，以及不能满足的条件。离线规划选择长期布局，运行时按实际状态重新检查；预测可以改变选择顺序，不能放宽身份、容量和完成条件。

## 先确定可共享的对象

一个可执行模型身份至少包含基座及版本、adapter 完整对象、数值表示、目标层、分片与布局。adapter 对象包含每个目标矩阵的 A/B、有效因子内维 r、缩放 s 和对象版本。相同模型名、相同形状或相同 r 都不足以证明对象相同。

采用列向量约定：

u＝Ax，y＝W₀x＋sBu，

其中 W₀∈R^{dₒ×dᵢ}、A∈R^{r×dᵢ}、B∈R^{dₒ×r}。r 是因子内维，rank(BA)≤r。固定 adapter 可形成 W′＝W₀＋sBA；运行时分支则在每个目标层共享基座矩阵乘，按请求加回各自增量，再把已加增量的隐藏状态传给下一层。不能先执行完整基座模型，最后才添加一次 adapter 修正。

合并副本减少运行时低秩分支，但复制完整权重或支付串行切换成本。共享基座保留跨 adapter 合批机会，却增加分组、低秩计算、对象加载和版本管理。实数恒等式不保证浮点逐位一致；合并、量化与分组路径必须满足同一声明的误差和质量要求。r＝0 时直接跳过增量，不能计算 α/r。

请求准入时固定绑定 β＝(请求生命期、租户、基座版本、adapter 版本、执行配置、状态身份)。路由别名更新只影响后续绑定。不同 adapter 下相同 token 可能产生不同 KV，即使 adapter 未直接修改 K/V 投影，上游隐藏状态也可能已经改变。默认把影响状态的 adapter 身份及版本纳入前缀身份；只有证明状态独立于某项依赖，才可省略。tokenizer、位置、模态内容和数值表示也需要相容性证明，不能由形状推断共享。

[S-LORA](../sources/S-LORA.md) 给出低秩分支及合并关系；[S-SLORA](../sources/S-SLORA.md) 将共享基座计算与异 adapter 分支分开。[S-VLLM-PREFIX](../sources/S-VLLM-PREFIX.md) 的固定文档将父块哈希、块 token 和额外身份共同用于前缀检索，明确包含 LoRA ID 并只缓存完整块。允许同一 ID 更新权重时，还须补充版本或内容身份。哈希检索、授权与真实计算完成是不同条件。

### 物理容量与逻辑份额

对设备 d，令 U_d(t) 是时刻 t 实际占用或已承诺的唯一物理 backing 集合，容量账为

M_d(t)＝Σ_{o∈U_d(t)} allocated_bytes(o)，max_t M_d(t)≤Cap_d。

对象包括权重、adapter、KV、执行区、图缓冲、加载目的区、在途缓冲、待消费输出，以及分配器已保留但未使用的物理空间。已承诺的空闲页以后变成存活对象时只改变分类，不再加第二份容量。纯虚拟地址预留不计物理驻留；未 backing 的增长需求要作为未来分配承诺检查。

容量键是设备与物理分配身份，不是内容哈希。同一基座 backing 被多个请求引用只计一次；同设备上两份内容相同但分配独立的副本仍计两次。同一物理键若出现不同大小或代次，必须先解决账本冲突，不能静默去重。

上述不等式是总字节约束。即使字节足够，连续区间、对齐、页大小、可写权限、图地址、分片或内核布局也可能不满足。只有实际页映射及生命期也已确定，才能认定这个具体计划可分配。保守上界超预算说明当前预留方案不能被该上界证明可行，不证明其他分块、串行或重算方案都不可能。

逻辑计费另设租户账。共享权重怎样分摊属于服务契约；不能把逻辑份额相加变成另一份物理权重，也不能用减少计费份额使活跃 KV 立即消失。借出的容量只有在请求结束、迁移、换出或重算路线实际释放后才可收回。

## 驻留、并行与路由的候选

独占副本便于归因和限制干扰，但低频模型可能长期闲置。完整模型共同驻留复用设备时间，却减少各模型的 KV 余量。冷模型按需加载以启动等待换容量，等待还包括旧版本排空、存储争用、转换、通信组建立与预热。共享基座的 LoRA 可只交换增量；极热且长期固定的 adapter 则可能适合合并副本。

模型并行提供另一种复用方式。层间流水把不同层放到不同设备，让连续请求同时占据不同阶段；在各层执行效率不变的假设下，它不缩短孤立请求的串行计算，还增加阶段通信。收益来自突发期间的流水吞吐和可用容量。算子内并行可以缩短单请求计算，却增加集合通信和同步。实际分片必须给出逐 rank 权重、复制张量、KV、workspace 和链路账，不能用组内总显存代替逐设备约束。

[AlpaServe v1](../sources/S-ALPASERVE.md) 研究模型并行与多模型统计复用，但主要评估一次前向的非自回归模型，不能把固定服务时间、batch 饱和或模拟器结果直接套到逐 token decode。执行组内一个设备故障可能破坏整个组；组内并行也不能替代不同故障域的独立副本。

### 两设备流水为何可能获益，也可能反转

以下是设定模型。模型 A/B 的完整权重各为 12 GiB；独占方案将 A 放设备 0、B 放设备 1。流水方案把两模型各分成两个 6 GiB 阶段：设备 0 保存 A₀/B₀，设备 1 保存 A₁/B₁，每设备权重仍为 12 GiB，执行区与请求状态另计。两个模型共享同一条 FIFO 流水，每设备一次执行一个阶段。

设单设备一次请求耗时 D＝10 ms；流水每阶段耗时 5.5 ms，已包含这一设定的阶段开销。四条 A 请求同时到达、B 没有请求时，独占方案完成时刻为 10、20、30、40 ms，均值 25 ms。流水在设备 0 依次运行 A₀，设备 1 在对应前阶段完成后运行 A₁，完成时刻为 11、16.5、22、27.5 ms，均值 19.25 ms。首条更慢，突发均值却下降。

若 A/B 同时各到达四条，独占方案的两设备同时工作，八条请求均值仍为 25 ms。共享流水的八个完成时刻从 11 ms 起每隔 5.5 ms 一个，均值变为 30.25 ms。两设备都持续饱和时，独占总服务率为 2/10 请求/ms，流水为 1/5.5 请求/ms，开销使后者更低。

因此应保留模型间突发的时间相关性。只给每模型平均到达率，或分别打乱轨迹，会删除决定复用收益的同时突发关系。真实 decode 还包含长度、KV、批组成和逐轮公平变化，需重新构建事件与资源模型。

## 放置与阶段划分怎样求解

### 先生成合法执行配置

设模型有 K 个保持拓扑顺序的层，候选流水阶段数为 S。对连续层段 [i,j)，预先给出阶段时间估计 ℓ(i,j) 和逐设备物理需求；不满足容量、布局或分片条件的层段标为不可行。在选择加性近似时，ℓ 可由逐层时间相加并加入相应通信；融合、cache 和不同并行配置改变时，必须重新校准，不能假设任意层段都可相加。

令 F(s,k) 表示前 k 层分成 s 个非空阶段时，能够得到的最小最大阶段时间：

F(0,0)＝0，其余未初始化状态为＋∞；

F(s,k)＝min_{s−1≤i<k，段[i,k)可行} max(F(s−1,i),ℓ(i,k))。

记录取得最小值的 i，从 F(S,K) 反向恢复所有阶段边界。不存在有限前驱即表示这个阶段数及配置下无解。空模型只接受零阶段；非空模型不允许零阶段或 S>K。时间复杂度为 O(SK²)，状态为 O(SK)，段成本准备另计。

例如层时间为 [6,1,1,4] ms，分两阶段。按层数均分得到 [6,1] 与 [1,4]，瓶颈 7 ms；动态规划得到 [6] 与 [1,1,4]，瓶颈 6 ms。若后者第二阶段容量不够，必须删去该分割，不能保留时间最优却无法分配的配置。

这个目标优化流水稳态间隔；孤立请求延迟还需加所有阶段及通信。阶段数增加也可能增加同时存活的激活、通信缓冲和状态版本，不能仅靠 F 值决定放置。

### 有限候选上的放置搜索

下面是从 AlpaServe 的配置枚举与模拟筛选思想推导的一种保守规划器，不声称复制其全部实现或找到全局最优。设备组在本候选族中互不重叠，同组允许驻留多个模型。其他共享组织可以另建候选。

目标先明确：在固定 offered 轨迹上，最大化满足数值、TTFT、ITL/完成时间等共同约束的完成请求数；另检查每租户拒绝率和份额约束。成本向量保留设备时间、加载字节、容量峰值与等待；没有指定偏好时不把异单位量直接相加。

```pseudocode
输入：有限模型/版本集合；有限设备分组与执行配置；固定请求轨迹；
      每设备容量、布局与链路条件；租户目标；束宽 B≥1；副本上限 R
输出：满足声明约束的最佳已发现计划，或未找到及逐候选原因

若模型集合为空，返回空计划；若配置集合为空，报告缺少候选
对每个设备分组及配置组合：
    用阶段划分和逐 rank 需求生成合法执行配置
    初始化 beam 为仅含空放置，best 保存当前可接受计划
    对深度 1 到 R：
        extensions ← 空集合
        对 beam 中每个计划 P：
            对每个有限的 (模型版本，设备组，执行配置)：
                构造增加一个副本的 P′，给独立 backing 新物理身份
                共享只在已有兼容 backing 确实被共同引用时去重
                建立权重、KV 承诺、workspace、加载与过渡版本生命期
                若逐设备字节、映射、执行身份或链路硬条件失败，记录并跳过
                按下述事件规则评估固定轨迹，保留所有拒绝与未完成请求
                以完整计划签名去重，把 P′ 加入 extensions
        若 extensions 为空，结束这个组合
        按预先声明的目标排序并保留前 B 个进入 beam
        仅当租户和服务约束满足时，更新 best；中间深度也可成为 best
合并所有组合的 best；返回已发现结果和适用轨迹
```

束搜索丢弃的分支可能包含更好方案；有限候选未找到结果不等于所有放置都不可行。物理需求随驻留和共享集合变化时，要在每个扩展中重算，不能固定一个“每模型大小”做所有装箱。

轨迹评估须展开执行依赖。对于固定 FIFO 流水，令 f(j,k) 是第 j 条请求在阶段 k 的完成时刻，阶段时间为 ℓ(j,k)：第一阶段等待请求到达及前一请求释放设备；后续阶段满足

f(j,k)＝max(f(j,k−1),f(j−1,k))＋ℓ(j,k)。

缺少的前驱视为初始设备空闲；加载和输入传输另作为必须完成的前驱。共享链路也有自己的占用时间，不能让两次传输各自使用独占带宽。真实模型有不同执行组或异构阶段时，使用对应设备和链路的事件依赖，不能继续套同一条 FIFO 递推。

逐 token 服务还要在本轮完成、采样和状态提交之后产生下一轮候选。每个时刻先处理已完成的资源事件，再处理到达并运行准入/轮转；只有真正完成的对象才可释放或供消费者使用。拒绝不从 offered 分母删除，窗口结束仍未完成的请求单列。服务时间是估计时，结果属于该模型的有限回放，不能称为未

增长一个 token 仍增加 3.75 MiB；忽略页舍入时，32 MiB 只够八轮共同增长，第九轮已越界。准入不能用“当前还放得下”代替持续推进的资源策略。

两个独立 12 GiB 合并副本已经用尽设备容量，无法容纳本例执行区与 KV。一个合并槽串行切换则可能合法，但需排空旧读者并计算合并、切换和等待成本。共享基座在这里扩大容量可行域，不单独证明服务目标达标。

### 计算与设备读取

一层总 query 数为 Q 时，基座线性层约需 2Qdᵢdₒ FLOPs；低秩分支约需

F_low＝2Σ_i q_i r_i(dᵢ＋dₒ)。

若统一补到 R≥max r_i，低秩主项变为 2Σ_i q_i R(dᵢ＋dₒ)。8 个 rank 16 与8 个 rank 64、q_i 相同时，实际维度和 640，补齐后 1024，低秩部分倍率为 1.6。它不适用于整个 forward。padding 还必须保持原 scale，不能把 α/r 改成 α/R。

权重逻辑读取主项为基座矩阵及活跃 adapter 的实际存储字节。一个融合批能否只从 HBM 读取一次基座，取决于 cache、分块和重读；不能把参数大小直接称为实测 DRAM 流量。共同前缀减少唯一 KV 驻留，但不同请求仍要取得各自可见历史。没有跨请求广播或片上复用证明，KV 读取不能按物理共享份数直接去重。

### 加载、通信、准备与同步

有效 H2D 带宽为 B、未命中对象总字节为 z 时，z/B 是相应共享链路的纯传输下界，另加存储、CPU 转换、页表、排队与同步。16 MiB 在 16 GiB/s 下为 0.9765625 ms；16 个不同未命中为 15.625 ms。若其他串行工作为 24 ms，关键路径为 39.625 ms，接近 40 ms ITL 上限。带宽降至 8 GiB/s 时变成 55.25 ms；忽略加载会错误保留这个候选。

若预取与当前计算能够重叠，理想阶段时间接近 max(T_compute,T_transfer)，再加不可隐藏的首尾和依赖；不能同时声称完全重叠又把两者全部相加。预取需要额外目的页和可能的 staging，错误预测增加流量并可能挤掉 KV。带宽竞争还可能让两条路径同时变慢。

流水每个边界传输的激活主项为 Qd_cut b_a 字节，其中 d_cut 是边界宽度，b_a 是激活元素字节；启动、链路争用与接收完成另计。TP 的元素量及 LoRA 分片取决于具体轴，须从已验证的执行配置取得，不能把总参数平均除以设备数。单设备候选没有模型内设备间通信，但用户输出传输仍进入端到端指标。

准备成本包括候选扫描、排序/轮转、对象检索、分组和行逆映射、页分配、图桶与描述填充。同步包括加载发布、阶段/collective 依赖、状态提交和最后使用回收。驻留成本既有峰值字节，也有对象长期占住容量的字节时间；后者需要结合被阻塞请求价值才能转换为服务代价。减少小算子可能同时增加等组时间，必须以完整请求时间线比较。

## 版本更新、取消与迟到完成的组合轨迹

继续用本例 16 MiB adapter。r1 已绑定 a:v1、正在读设备页 p1；r2 将绑定 a:v2。旧版本仍在途时，v2 的新 backing 至少再占 16 MiB，可能还需独立 staging。若共同预算仅剩 32 MiB，双版本已经消耗其中一半；不能把 v1 的预期释放提前用于 v2 的承诺。

1. r1 固定 β_r1 和 p1 的页代次，持有逻辑引用；执行提交登记独立操作 ID，取得实际读权。缓存目录是否保留对象另记。
2. 发布路由别名 a→v2，新请求绑定 v2，r1 的绑定保持 v1。预留 p2 与 staging，登记复制操作，v2 为 FETCHING。
3. r2 可以进入有完整承诺的待加载状态；复制成功并核对 A/B、scale、布局与全 rank 对象一致后，v2 才 READY。r2 的实际执行在其后提交。
4. r1 取消后停止新业务提交和交付，释放可结束的逻辑责任，并撤销不再需要的目录资格；旧执行仍保有 p1 的实际读权。
5. 旧执行完成事件按操作 ID 和页代次结算一次。重复事件没有第二次扣减效果，不能减少 p2 或后来复用 p1 的新操作责任。
6. p1 无逻辑引用、无目录保留或已合法撤销目录、无在途读写后才可回收。复用 p1 时增加页代次，旧通知不能作用于新代。
7. 若 r2 在复制期间取消，未提交执行，但复制写者仍须排空；完成后释放失败请求的承诺。对象可否继续留给其他请求由仍存活的引用决定。

反例是将 p1 原地改成 v2，再让已提交的 r1 继续读取同一地址。路由表正确也救不了旧读者，其实际结果已经改变。另一个反例是在复制取消时立即复用 p2，迟到 DMA 会覆盖新对象。独立页、写时复制或其他方案都可以，但必须保留旧读写者的完成关系。

## 条件变化与区分实验

| 观察或条件变化 | 竞争解释或保留条件 | 区分干预与反证后的修正 |
|---|---|---|
| 模型并行在部分轨迹上更快 | 突发互补减少等待；更高带宽或更好分片也可能降低服务时间 | 固定阶段服务时间，只改变模型间到达相关性；同时突发使收益消失时，应收窄统计复用结论 |
| 混合 adapter 吞吐下降 | 冷加载、小 kernel、准备开销、页压力或基座饱和 | 固定 offered 轨迹，分别预驻留、改变分组及增加可用页；预驻留后仍慢则撤回纯加载解释 |
| rank 桶增大后变慢 | padding 算术、图变体或驻留挤掉 KV | 固定有效 rank，仅改桶宽，分记低秩执行、准备、准入和等待；只有排队增加不能归为 FLOPs |
| 缓存命中提高但 TTFT 变差 | 亲和路由集中、热页占容量或冷对象等待 | 固定真实命中边界改变路由，再固定路由改变驻留；按等待发生位置修正解释 |
| 同文本换 adapter 后输出错误 | 身份漏版本、错误可写页或位置/数值表示不符 | 用独立完整输入计算参考，关闭复用，再只改变 adapter；错误随非法命中出现才支持身份解释 |
| 更新或取消后旧结果变化 | 原地覆盖、混合 A/B 发布、提前回收或旧事件扣新引用 | 延迟真实读者/复制完成，比较保留旧 backing 与提前复用的负对照；字段正确但内容变化仍判失败 |

数值检查应比较每个 adapter 的独立执行与共享执行，覆盖异 rank、同 rank 异对象、零增量和行重排；这些线性与分片细节见[多 LoRA 执行](../algorithms/lora-serving.md)。目标设备实验另需验证真实布局、allocator、异步可见性、kernel、链路争用及数值路径。

随章 tools/check_k_work_007_full.py 是确定性、只读、离线的 Python 标准库模型。它以显式物理槽集合核对容量，以枚举所有切分核对阶段动态规划，以合法集合参考核对路由，以持续就绪窗口核对轮转，并实际制造旧读者内容改变的负对照。它还保留旧路由并列用例，检查严格最短非法候选、容量阈值、增长、传输和回收代次。软件模型通过不能证明 GPU 测量结果、未来总体 SLO 或知识改善了 Agent 的构建效果。

成本和能耗回答“交付相同质量与时延要求的结果，消耗了多少资源”。峰值吞吐、最大设备利用率与最低瞬时功率都不能独立回答这个问题。比较前先固定 offered workload、输出工作量、质量和服务目标，再定义合格完成的分母。

## 成本的系统边界

在观察窗口内，将设备与主机占用、存储容量/请求、网络流量以及确定需要单独计价的项目相加。设备占用应包括加载、预热、等待、排空、失败重试与必要热备用；已有包价包含的主机或电力不能再次加一遍。价格由用户给定或绑定明确合同与日期，本知识库不写死现价。

若窗口成本为 C，满足指定质量、首 token、ITL/完成时延条件的请求数为 N_good，则每合格请求成本为 C/N_good。N_good=0 时该指标不可用，不能报告为零成本。对输出长度不同的任务，可另报每合格 token、每图像或每音频秒，但必须保留其质量、长度和到达分布，不能用缩短输出获得表面的单位优势。

多租户共享基座时，物理总成本和逻辑分摊应分开。按照请求数、设备时间、KV 驻留或保留容量分摊，会给出不同的租户成本；分摊规则属于服务契约，不能把没有实际减少的设备时间当作节省。对暂时闲置但必须保留的故障容量，也要说明计入谁的目标。

## 能量、功率与计量域

能量是观察区间内功率的积分。平均功率低而运行更久，可能消耗更多能量。可以测总能耗，也可以报告相对空闲基线的增量能耗；二者回答不同问题，必须同时写清系统边界和基线。设备板卡、CPU package、DRAM、整机入口和机房设施不是同一个计量域。

[Linux 6.12 powercap](../sources/S-LINUX-RESOURCES.md) 定义了能量计数、计数范围及分层 power zone。RAPL 的 package 与子域存在包含关系，不能盲目把所有层级读数相加。该接口中的能量单位为微焦耳；它不等于对每个请求直接计量，也不保证所有平台暴露相同域。控制功率上限的窗口参数同样不代表实际瞬时功率。

使用累计计数时，先核对单位、计数范围、重置和采样间隔。只有确认至多一次回绕且没有重置，才能由两次读数与范围恢复差值；长时间间隔中多次回绕、进程迁移或计量域变化会使简单差分失效。请求并行时，把整机能量按吞吐均分是归因方法，不能称作单请求物理测量。

## 选择频率、批量与冗余

降低频率或功率限制可能降低 P，也可能延长计算、放大队列和降低 N_good；增加 batch 可能摊薄权重读取与主机开销，也可能增加等待和峰值内存。把热备用关掉能减少闲置能量，却增加冷启动失败和首 token 超时。应比较满足共同约束的候选，或画出成本、能量与服务质量的可行边界。

硬件采购、租赁价格和电价属于不同决策模型。短期任务可用实际计费单位；长期自建需显式给定摊销和利用率假设。若所比较的目标是设备时间或焦耳，可先报告这些可复核量，避免让价格假设掩盖机制。

## 一个成本与能量同时反转的算例

以下价格、功率与请求数均为设定值。两候选在同样一小时、同样 offered workload 下运行：A 总设备与主机成本 4 单位，合格完成 10,000 请求；B 成本 3 单位，合格完成 6,000 请求。A 为 0.0004 单位/合格请求，B 为 0.0005；B 的每小时费用更低，却没有更低的合格结果成本。若 B 经合法调度在同样成本下完成 9,000 个合格请求，单位成本才降至约 0.000333。

再设同一完整计量域内 A 的平均功率为 500 W，B 为 350 W，测量区间均为一小时。A 消耗 1.8 MJ、180 J/合格请求；B 消耗 1.26 MJ、210 J/合格请求。较低平均功率没有带来更高的有效能量效率。若空闲基线均为 100 W，增量指标分别为 144 与 150 J/合格请求；这些增量值不包含全部运行能量，不应替代总能耗披露。

## 验证与可迁移的结论

记录计费或资源占用区间与能量测量区间是否一致，包含启动和结束后的必要排空。对动态功率，按时间戳积分并检查漏采、回绕、重置及设备身份。用已知持续功率的合成数据验证单位换算，再对目标平台校验不同计量域，不能把合成算例当作硬件测量。

重复实验应采用共同负载与独立保留样本，报告拒绝、质量失败、超时和取消，并按[实验统计](../tools/statistical-experiments.md)处理运行间波动。只有在相同服务条件下资源用量下降，才支持机制层面的效率结论；价格、空闲占比、故障余量或输出长度改变后，需要重新计算选择。

## 资源向量与可行集合

一个实例的需求可表示为逐 rank 的 GPU 类型与内存、CPU 时间/核集合、主存、临时存储、NIC 与带宽，以及 rank 之间的连接要求。设备算力、容量和网络不能直接相加成一个没有单位的总分。先排除不满足硬约束的位置，再比较剩余候选的排队、成本与干扰。

总 GPU 内存不能替代每 rank 预算：参数切片之外，部分张量可能复制，workspace 与 KV 也会不均衡。相同型号但不同链路、NUMA 或 quota 的设备，实际执行成本不同。编译与内核支持属于能力约束；某台机器能安装相同容器，不证明它能执行同一指令路径。

[Borg](../sources/S-BORG.md) 区分配额准入、资源可行性和位置评分，并讨论紧凑装箱与碎片、包局部性、故障域之间的关系。这些是集群层机制；将其用于 GPU 推理时，仍需加入设备组、状态和通信约束，不能把论文中的 CPU 混部效果当作推理性能保证。

## 共同启动与控制状态

TP/PP/EP 组中的 rank 需要形成相容的执行集合。可以先预留整个组，再加载和建立通信；也可以分阶段取得资源，但要限制部分取得后长期占用且无法完成的情况。这里的 gang 准入指整组满足启动条件后才作为服务容量公开，不要求所有操作在同一个物理时刻发生。

控制面拥有期望的副本、放置和版本；节点报告实际分配、加载与执行状态。计划基于旧观察时可能失效，提交放置必须重新检查资源与代次。路由读取的是已就绪实例集合，不能直接把“调度已决定”当作“模型可计算”。调度器故障与已有数据面是否继续工作，也需要明确约定。

## 碎片与两种放置比较

设定四个节点各有 4 张同型 GPU，目前每个节点各剩 2 张空闲，总空闲为 8 张。新服务 A 的验证方案要求同一节点 4 卡，另一服务 B 每副本只需 1 卡。A 仍然不可放置，B 可在这些空位运行；为 B 填满全部余量又可能延长 A 等待完整节点的时间。

候选一保留即将释放的完整节点给 A，把 B 放到其他位置，代价是暂时留空部分卡。候选二将 A 改为两个节点各 2 卡，需重新核对跨节点通信、组装与故障条件。只有在新的执行布局和 SLO 验证通过后，第二种方案才是合法替代；不能用总空闲数量跳过这一验证。迁移已有任务以消除碎片，还要计入迁移带宽、排空及受影响服务的代价。

紧凑放置可为大型实例保留完整空间，也可能集中争用 CPU、NIC 与 SSD。分散放置减少局部干扰和相关失败，但可能扩大通信距离、减少权重缓存命中或造成小碎片。[多模型放置](multi-model-placement.md) 与[路由迁移](../algorithms/routing-and-migration.md)决定这些代价是否值得支付。

## 故障域与可用容量

副本是功能上的替代，只有分散到适当故障域才具有相应容错价值。同一节点的两个模型实例可能同时失去 CPU、驱动或网络；不同节点但共用机架网络、供电或存储出口，也仍有共同故障。执行组内部追求近距离通信，独立副本之间追求故障分散，二者需要分别设计。

设定三个副本组各能处理 40 请求/s，正常到达为 70 请求/s。丢失任一组后剩余 80 请求/s，仅从平均服务率看仍有余量，尾延迟是否达标仍需测量。如果两个副本共用同一故障域且会同时失去，剩余只有 40 请求/s，就无法维持这个到达率。此时要增加独立余量、调整放置或承诺故障时的降载/拒绝。

超售也需按资源区别处理。空闲 CPU 时间可能通过节流交回，但正在使用的 GPU 权重与 KV 不能凭降低调度权重立即消失。把内存容量超售给不可抢占的请求，会将配额争用转成 OOM；可借用容量应绑定明确可撤回的状态和代价。

## 可区分方案的验证

以具体部署描述检查每个 rank 的容量、设备身份、通信集合和允许的路径，再用保留轨迹比较放置方案。记录待调度原因、碎片、启动各阶段、网络/存储热点与逐租户 SLO。模拟或注入一个 rank、一台主机、一个共享存储出口不可用，确认故障后哪些组仍完整、路由何时停止指向旧代次，以及剩余容量的实际工作量。

模型很小、独占实例长期低负载时，混部收益可能占优；大模型需要完整高速设备组、严格尾延迟或强故障隔离时，保留空间和拓扑约束更重要。集群设计的目标是兑现推理契约，而不是单独优化装箱率。

## 先定义对象契约

| 对象 | 主要读取/更新模式 | 丢失后的恢复条件 |
|---|---|---|
| 模型、adapter、tokenizer 与量化制品 | 版本内只读，分片/范围读取，批量分发 | 从可信且完整的相同版本重新取得；缺片不能继续发布 |
| 可复用 KV 或中间状态 | 按前缀/层/块读取，逐步产生或封闭 | 只有保留完整输入、模型身份和恢复语义时才可重算 |
| embedding 与检索索引 | 查询、批量构建、增量更新或整体替换 | 需要原始文档、embedding 版本、索引参数与删除/更新记录 |

| 临时 staging、可再生编译缓存 | 短期读写，格式与环境绑定 | 可删除重建，但重建成本和峰值必须进入启动预算 |

可重算只描述恢复路线，不等于恢复免费。缓存丢失后集中重算会争用 CPU/GPU，影响仍正常的请求；索引重建还可能包含长时间的数据扫描。某些递归状态、工具结果和随机过程无法仅凭文本恢复，必须明确保留范围。

## 对象、文件与块的接口选择

对象接口用键与版本定位整体对象或范围，适合不可变分片和分发，但不能假设跨多个对象的原子发布或目录 rename 语义。文件接口提供路径、偏移与文件系统操作，具体原子性、缓存可见性和持久性仍依赖所选实现。块接口提供地址空间与 I/O，文件布局、版本和发布由上层负责。

这些接口不是天然的快慢顺序。大量小元数据请求可能限制启动，大对象顺序读则可能受出口带宽限制。范围读取是否真正减少下游字节、直接 I/O 的对齐与并发条件、mmap 是否产生缺页或双重缓存，都要接回[存储 I/O](../hardware/storage-io.md)与[加载布局](../frameworks/checkpoint-loading.md)。

[Ceph 2006](../sources/S-CEPH06.md) 展示数据与元数据路径分离、计算式放置、跨故障域副本以及可见确认和落盘提交的区别。它是机制来源；当时原型的安全协议和 MDS 恢复尚未完整实现，不能据此承诺当前后端的 API、可靠性或性能。

## 完整版本如何发布与读取

写入者先产生不可变分片，再检查完整集合的大小、表示和必要内容校验，最后发布能引用全部已完成对象的版本清单。读者先取得一个确定的清单版本，再按该版本读取所有分片；不能在每次读取时重新解析可能变化的 latest 指针，从而把新旧权重拼在一起。

发布指针的原子性需要所选存储提供明确操作，或由外部权威记录维护；没有跨对象事务时，不应假装多次上传天然原子。部分写入失败留在未发布集合，重试不会让半成品进入可读版本。回退改动新请求的版本选择，旧读者仍须能够完成；删除旧版本应等待实际读者和保留策略允许。

数据已到客户端内存、已被多个副本接收、可供其他客户端读取、已达到所需持久性，是不同完成点。对请求提交日志尤其要说明何时可以对外承诺成功；对可重算缓存则可以选择较弱持久性并承受 miss，但有效性和租户身份检查不能因此省掉。

## 分发、复制与恢复的共同带宽

设定一个制品 32 GiB，16 个节点同时从共享出口获取，出口有效读带宽为 8 GiB/s。没有本地命中或对等分发时，总出口需要交付 512 GiB，最后全部取得的纯传输下界为 64 s，不能为每节点都使用 4 s 的独占估计。若每机已有一份相同版本的本地缓存，出口流量可减少，但本地读、校验、转换与 H2D 仍在关键路径。

树形或对等分发减少集中出口压力，代价是节点间链路、临时存储和额外失败路径；收到的内容仍须属于同一清单版本。缓存可以合并并发 miss，避免相同分片被重复拉取，但取消一个等待者不能误删其他等待者还需要的共享下载。

容量账要区分逻辑数据与副本。设逻辑制品 100 GiB、三副本，则数据主项已为 300 GiB，尚未包含元数据、旧版本、恢复过程的新副本与临时写入。恢复和重平衡还会消费在线读取所需的磁盘和网络；后端报告“可恢复”不等于恢复期间仍满足原来的启动或 KV 延迟。

## 故障验证与选择反转

测试缺片、截断、错误版本、过期目录、部分范围完成、读过程中版本切换、旧版本清理、共享下载取消、节点失效和恢复流量并发。成功条件是读者只得到完整且相容的对象，失败可以定位到阶段，原有有效副本的责任没有提前消失。

性能分别测元数据操作、冷读/热读、范围读取、并发启动与恢复期尾延迟。权重长期稳定且节点重复启动时，本地缓存更有价值；模型版本频繁变化或节点短命时，共享源与分发效率更关键。对 KV，比较远端恢复、压缩和重算的完整费用；对不可丢的提交状态，则先满足协议的持久性要求，再优化路径。
